days.title: Requirements to Code, and Predictable, Secure Configuration

concepts.heading: Turning a Requirement into One Source of Truth
concepts.body: At professional level a requirement such as 'every resource carries owner, cost-center and environment tags, and the cost center changes in exactly one place' is a request to remove duplication. The language tool is a local value: `locals { common_tags = { Owner = var.owner, CostCenter = var.cost_center, Environment = var.environment } }` defines the map once, and each resource adds its own keys with `merge(local.common_tags, { Name = "web" })`. Changing `var.cost_center` changes every consumer in the next plan. Locals may reference variables and other locals, but a variable cannot be declared inside a resource block, and the `terraform` block takes constants only. The same idea builds names: `locals { name_prefix = "${var.org}-${var.environment}-${var.app}" }` constructs the string once, so a convention such as org-env-app cannot drift between resources. Construction alone does not stop a caller from passing nonsense, so pair it with a constraint. A default merely supplies a value when none is given, and a comment is never checked by Terraform. Policy that must hold has to be encoded, not described.

concepts.heading: Fail at the Input with Validation
concepts.body: A `validation` block on a variable evaluates its `condition` while Terraform builds the plan. When it is false the run stops and prints `error_message`. No provider call has happened yet, so nothing is created. Typical conditions are `contains(["dev", "stage", "prod"], var.environment)`, `can(regex("^[a-z]+$", var.name))` and numeric ranges. A requirement such as 'production instances may only be m5.large, m5.xlarge or m5.2xlarge, reported before any resource exists' therefore belongs on the variable. In current Terraform versions a validation condition may also refer to other input variables, locals and data sources, so a cross-field rule like `condition = var.max_size >= var.min_size` on `max_size` rejects the bad pair at the variable that was wrong. A `precondition` on a resource can express the same rule, but it reports the problem where the value is consumed, not where it was supplied. A description is documentation only, `ignore_changes` tells Terraform to ignore drift (the opposite of enforcing), and an output is evaluated after the fact and enforces nothing.

concepts.heading: Which Assertion Blocks the Run
concepts.body: Terraform has several assertion constructs and the exam asks which one actually stops a pipeline. `precondition` and `postcondition` live in the `lifecycle` block of resources and data sources; an `output` block can also hold a `precondition` directly, but outputs take no postcondition. A precondition is evaluated before the object is acted on and cannot use `self`; a postcondition runs afterwards, may use `self`, and objects that depend on it are not processed until it passes. Both stop the run when false. A `check` block with `assert` validates whole-infrastructure assumptions on an ongoing basis, but a failed assertion only produces a warning and never blocks plan or apply. Variable `validation` checks inputs only. Scenario: reviewers want a violation to block the apply when a subnet module is used with a non-private subnet. A check block fails that goal because it only warns; a precondition (or validation on the input) fits. Another: a data source finds an AMI and no instance may be built from a non-arm64 image. The architecture is known only after the lookup and dependents must not proceed, so the postcondition goes on the data source.

concepts.heading: Optional Resources, Data Sources and Composition
concepts.body: Requirements often describe things that exist only sometimes or that already exist. For optional resources, `count = var.environment == "prod" ? 1 : 0` is the standard toggle, but the resource then becomes a list. With zero instances `cpu[0]` fails with an invalid-index error, and with no index at all Terraform reports that the resource needs an instance key. The splat `cpu[*].arn` always yields a list, and `one()` converts a list of zero or one elements to `null` or that element (two or more is an error), so `one(aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm.cpu[*].arn)` is defined in both cases. For existing facts use a data source: `data "aws_ami"` with `most_recent = true` and a tag filter resolves the newest approved image at each plan, removes a stale hard-coded ID, and a precondition or postcondition states the assumption with your own message. Composition is the last decision. A platform team that owns the shared network and many application teams that deploy into it should use separate root modules, each with its own state and plan, linked by published outputs (for example through a remote state data source) or by tag-filtered data sources, so the network can change without touching application state.

concepts.heading: Predictable and Secure: Pinning, Sensitivity and Least Privilege
concepts.body: Predictability comes from two layers of pinning. `required_providers` constraints say which versions are acceptable, and the docs recommend `~>` in root modules to set both a bound below and above. The dependency lock file `.terraform.lock.hcl` records the exact version and checksums chosen by `terraform init`; later inits reuse them until `terraform init -upgrade`. Commit it and a change becomes a reviewable diff. `required_version = "~> 1.12.0"` constrains the CLI only: with 1.14.2 installed, init fails with an unsupported-Terraform-version error and never fetches another CLI. A git module source with no `ref` uses the default branch, so a merged change breaks tomorrow's plan; use `?ref=v2.3.1`, because the `version` argument works only for registry sources and the lock file covers providers, not modules. Sensitivity propagates: an output built from a sensitive variable fails with an error that the output refers to sensitive values until the output is also `sensitive = true` (or the value is deliberately wrapped in `nonsensitive()`). Sensitive hides display only; it is still stored in state. Least privilege means specific actions such as `s3:GetObject` on the real ARN (`aws_s3_bucket.data.arn` plus the path), never `s3:*` on `*`.

examPoints: A question where a rule must be reported 'before any resource is created' points to variable validation (or a precondition); a resource that merely warns points to a check block, which never blocks plan or apply.

A question about `required_version` versus providers versus modules is testing which pin covers what: required_version limits the CLI, required_providers plus the lock file pin providers, and `?ref=` pins a git module source.
A question where an output fails with an error that the output refers to sensitive values wants the output marked sensitive; remember that sensitive only hides display and the value remains in state.

quiz.q: A security standard requires owner, cost-center and environment tags on every resource, with the cost-center value changeable in exactly one place. Which design in the root module meets this?
choices: Define the tags in a `locals` map built from variables and add resource-specific keys with `merge(local.common_tags, {...})`
Declare a `variable` block inside each resource block and set the same default value in every one of them
Copy the tag map into each resource and describe the single source of truth in a comment above the first block
Place the cost-center value in the `terraform` block so that every resource block in the module can read it
quiz.explain: A local defines the map once and merge adds per-resource keys, so one edit reaches every consumer. Choice B is impossible because variables are not declared inside resource blocks, and choice D fails because the terraform block accepts constants only.

quiz.q: A module has an output that fails with an error that the output refers to sensitive values because it embeds `var.db_password`, which is `sensitive = true`. A reviewer also asks whether the password is protected in state. Which statement is accurate?
choices: Marking the output sensitive fixes the error, and sensitive also encrypts the value, so state holds no readable password
Marking the output sensitive fixes the error, but the value is still stored in state and `terraform output -json` prints it
Wrapping the value in `nonsensitive()` fixes the error and keeps the password hidden in CLI output as well as in state
Removing `sensitive` from the variable fixes the error, because outputs are never allowed to derive from a sensitive input
quiz.explain: Sensitivity only redacts display; state keeps the value and -json or -raw output shows it in plain text. Choice C is wrong because nonsensitive() removes the mark, so the password would print.

days.recap: Encode requirements instead of describing them: locals build values once, validation rejects bad input at plan, preconditions and postconditions block while check only warns. Pin the CLI, providers (constraints plus committed lock file) and git modules separately, and remember sensitive hides display but not state.

days.title: Tracing Variables, Locals, Outputs and for_each Instances

concepts.heading: Follow the Value Hop by Hop
concepts.body: Tracing a configuration bug means walking the chain the value should travel: tfvars or CLI gives the root variable, the variable feeds a local, the local feeds a resource argument, and for module calls the root must pass the value explicitly to the child. Every module, root or child, has its own input variables, and nothing is shared by name. If the root sets `instance_type = "m5.xlarge"` in tfvars but the call is just `module "app" { source = "./app" }`, the child falls back to its own default (t3.micro) and instances stay small. The fix is `instance_type = var.instance_type` inside the module block. `terraform plan` shows the arguments of the module's resources and so shows where the chain stops, and `terraform console` lets you evaluate each hop. Where variables may appear matters too: the backend block is read at `terraform init`, before variables exist, so it cannot use variables or locals (use partial configuration with `-backend-config`), and the `terraform` block takes constants only. A provider `region = var.region` or an output built from a variable is normal.

concepts.heading: null, Empty Strings and nullable
concepts.body: Wrong values often come from confusing null with empty. `null` means no value; `""` is a real string. A local such as `name = var.name != null ? var.name : "${var.app}-svc"` evaluates `var.name != null` as true when tfvars contains `name = ""`, so the empty string flows into the local and then into every resource. Treat both as missing with `var.name != null && var.name != ""`, or use `coalesce(var.name, "${var.app}-svc")`, which skips null and empty strings. Variable declarations add a second layer. By default a variable is `nullable = true`, so a caller that passes `null` sends null through and the default is not used. With `nullable = false` and a default, passing null makes Terraform use the default; with `nullable = false` and no default, passing null is an error. That is why a module author who sees a surprise null should check both what the caller forwards (a caller that forwards its own `var.x` may be sending null deliberately) and how the module declared the variable.

concepts.heading: Closed Boxes, Counts and Cycles
concepts.body: A module's resources are private. Only declared outputs leave it, and a caller reads `module.<name>.<output_name>`. The expression `module.network.aws_subnet.private.id` fails with an unsupported-attribute error because the module object has no such attribute; add `output "private_subnet_id" { value = aws_subnet.private.id }` inside the module and use `module.network.private_subnet_id`. When `count` is set, `aws_instance.web` is a list: a bare `aws_instance.web.id` fails with an error that the resource needs an instance key, `aws_instance.web[0].id` selects one, and `aws_instance.web[*].id` collects all. With `for_each` the resource is a map keyed by instance key, so you use `["a"]` or a `for` expression. Dependency cycles are a third trace: every reference is a graph edge, so `locals { a = "x-${local.b}", b = "y-${local.a}" }` cannot be ordered and plan stops with a cycle error naming both locals. Break the loop by deriving both from a variable, a resource attribute or one shared local. `depends_on` cannot be used on locals and would add edges rather than remove them.

concepts.heading: count Positions Versus for_each Keys
concepts.body: Terraform tracks instances by address. With `count` the address is a position: `[0]`, `[1]`, `[2]`. Instances created with `count = length(var.names)` for [a, b, c] shift when b is removed: the list becomes [a, c], so index 1 (previously b) is updated or, if the changed attribute is immutable such as a bucket name, replaced to become c, and index 2 is destroyed. With names changing from [a, b, c] to [b, c], every remaining position needs a new name, so the plan replaces two and destroys one. With `for_each = toset(var.names)` the addresses are keys (`["a"]`, `["b"]`, `["c"]`), so removing b removes only `["b"]`. `for_each` accepts a map or a set of strings, not a list: a `list(string)` fails with an error naming the type, and the fix is `toset()` or a `for` expression building a map. Duplicates collapse in a set, so two equal strings give one instance. Use a map when each instance needs its own settings, with `each.key` and `each.value`. `count` and `for_each` cannot be used in the same block.

concepts.heading: for_each Keys: Known Early, Unique and Not Secret
concepts.body: Instance keys must be known at plan time because Terraform needs every address before it contacts providers. A `for_each` built from `toset([for s in aws_subnet.private : s.id])` fails on a new environment with an error that the keys cannot be determined until apply, since IDs are created during apply. Take keys from values you control (a variable, a local, a literal map), or iterate the resource itself: `for_each = aws_subnet.private` works because its keys are the original static keys. `-target` can bypass the error once but leaves a permanent two-step apply. In a `{ for s in var.subnets : s.name => s }` expression, two entries with name "app" cause a duplicate-object-key error; the ellipsis (`...`) groups values into lists, but the better fix is a unique key. Keys are part of the address, so renaming `"web-a"` to `"web-1"` plans a destroy and a create; a `moved` block `from = aws_instance.web["web-a"]`, `to = aws_instance.web["web-1"]` retargets the state with no real change. A sensitive map cannot be used directly in `for_each`; extract non-secret keys with `toset([for k, v in var.users : k])` and read `var.users[each.key]` inside.

examPoints: A question where a tfvars value is set but the deployment ignores it is usually a missing argument in the `module` block: values do not cross module boundaries by name.
A question where removing an item from the middle of a list destroys or replaces later resources is testing count positions; the cure is for_each keys, and a key rename needs a moved block.
A question quoting 'cannot be determined until apply' for for_each is testing that keys must come from values known at plan time, not from generated IDs.

quiz.q: A module declares `variable "name" { type = string, default = "svc", nullable = false }`. The caller passes `name = null`. What does the module use for `var.name`, and what happens if the same variable had the default `nullable = true`?
choices: With `nullable = false` the module uses `"svc"`; with the default `nullable = true` the module sees `null`
The module uses `"svc"` in both cases, because a default is applied whenever the caller passes no usable value
The module sees `null` in both cases, because a default only applies when the variable is left out of the module block
Terraform reports an error in both cases, because passing `null` to a string variable is never accepted by a module
quiz.explain: nullable = false makes Terraform substitute the default for null, while the default nullable = true passes null through. Choice B is tempting because defaults feel automatic, but null is treated as a value unless nullable is false.

quiz.q: A list `var.names` is [a, b, c] and a bucket resource uses `count = length(var.names)` with `bucket = var.names[count.index]`. The list becomes [b, c] and a bucket name change forces replacement. What does the plan show?
choices: One bucket destroyed (a) and the other two kept unchanged, because Terraform matches buckets by name
Two buckets replaced (index 0 and 1 get new names) and one destroyed (index 2), because instances are matched by position
No changes at all, because count only reads the list length and ignores the values inside the list
The plan fails with a duplicate address error, because index 2 no longer exists in the new list of names
quiz.explain: count addresses are positions, so index 0 now wants b and index 1 wants c, both immutable changes, and index 2 disappears. Choice A describes what for_each over toset would do.

days.recap: Trace a wrong value along tfvars, root variable, module argument, child variable and resource argument, and remember modules only expose outputs. Null differs from an empty string, count is positional while for_each is keyed, and for_each keys must be known at plan time, unique and not sensitive.

days.title: Predicting Function Results and Collection Expressions

concepts.heading: CIDR Functions: Count Addresses, Not Octets
concepts.body: `cidrsubnet(prefix, newbits, netnum)` extends the prefix length by `newbits` and picks subnet number `netnum`, counting from zero. For `cidrsubnet("10.1.0.0/16", 4, 3)`: /16 plus 4 new bits is /20, and there are 2^4 = 16 such subnets. A /20 holds 4,096 addresses, which is 16 steps of 256 in the third octet, so subnet N starts at third octet `N * 16`: subnet 0 is `10.1.0.0/20`, subnet 1 is `10.1.16.0/20`, and subnet 3 is `10.1.48.0/20`. The classic mistake is to use the newbits count (3 x 4 = 12) as the step. `cidrhost(prefix, hostnum)` returns the address at position `hostnum` in the prefix, counting from the network address as 0, and negative numbers count backward from the end. `10.0.8.0/22` covers `10.0.8.0` to `10.0.11.255`, 1,024 addresses, so host 260 (256 + 4) spills into the next third octet and gives `10.0.9.4`. Only a number beyond the range, here above 1,023, is an error. When asked to predict a result, work out the block size first and then the position.

concepts.heading: merge Is Shallow; try, can and coalesce Differ
concepts.body: `merge` combines maps or objects from left to right, and for each top-level key the last argument that has it wins, replacing the whole value. `merge({ tags = { env = "prod", team = "net" } }, { tags = { env = "dev" } }).tags` is `{ env = "dev" }`: the nested object is replaced as a unit and `team` disappears. To combine nested maps, merge them explicitly: `{ tags = merge(a.tags, b.tags) }`. `try(expr1, expr2, ...)` returns the first argument that does not raise an error, which is not the same as the first non-null one. With `local.cfg = { db = { port = null } }`, `try(local.cfg.db.port, 5432)` returns `null`, because the attribute exists and reading it is not an error; a missing attribute would raise an unsupported-attribute error and fall back. The docs recommend `try` sparingly since it hides typos. `can(expr)` returns a boolean for whether the expression evaluates without error and is mainly used in validation conditions. Neither intercepts provider failures, which occur later. `coalesce("", null, "eu-west-1", "us-east-1")` returns `eu-west-1`: it skips both null and empty strings, errors if all are empty, and `coalescelist` is the list version.

concepts.heading: Shaping Lists and Sets: flatten, concat, toset, element
concepts.body: Know what each list function does to nesting and order. `flatten` removes all levels of nesting from a list of lists, however deep, keeping order. `concat` joins lists end to end but does not flatten, so a list given as an element stays nested. `distinct` drops duplicates, keeping the first occurrence and the original order. `compact` removes empty strings and nulls from a list of strings. `slice(list, start, end)` returns elements from `start` up to but not including `end`. `toset` converts a list to a set, coalescing duplicates and discarding the order, so `toset(["b", "a", "b"])` has two elements and a `for_each` over it creates `res["a"]` and `res["b"]`. Use `distinct` when you want unique elements but need the original order. `element(list, index)` takes the index modulo the list length, so it cycles: with `local.azs = ["a", "b", "c"]`, `element(local.azs, 4)` is `"b"` (4 mod 3 is 1), while `local.azs[4]` is an invalid-index error. This round-robin spreads numbered instances over a short zone list, but adding a zone in the middle shifts the cycle for existing instances. `setproduct(var.envs, var.regions)` returns every combination as a list of lists: 2 x 3 gives 6 elements.

concepts.heading: for Expressions: Braces, Brackets and the Ellipsis
concepts.body: A `for` expression in square brackets produces a tuple of results with no keys; in braces it produces an object or map, with one key and one value per iteration. In an object-producing expression each key must be unique. `{ for s in ["ab", "cd", "ae"] : substr(s, 0, 1) => s }` fails with a duplicate-object-key error for `"a"`, and Terraform notes that the ellipsis may be used if duplicates are expected. Adding `...` after the value, `substr(s, 0, 1) => s...`, switches on grouping mode and gives `{ a = ["ab", "ae"], c = ["cd"] }`. Notice that with grouping every value is a list, even `c`, which occurs once; without grouping every value is a scalar. Grouping changes the value type, so downstream resources must handle lists; often the better fix is to make the key unique, for example `"${s.vpc}-${s.name}"`. Silent overwrite would hide a configuration bug, so Terraform never does it. For a Cartesian `for_each`, `{ for p in setproduct(var.envs, var.regions) : "${p[0]}-${p[1]}" => p }` works because `for_each` accepts only a map or set of strings, not a list of lists, and the keys such as `prod-eu` stay stable when other pairs change.

concepts.heading: File and Template Functions
concepts.body: `file(path)` reads a file as UTF-8 text and returns the string. A binary file such as a PKCS#12 bundle is not valid UTF-8, so `file("${path.module}/bundle.p12")` fails with an invalid UTF-8 error. `filebase64(path)` reads raw bytes and returns them Base64-encoded, the right way to carry archives, keystores or images in an argument. Wrapping `file()` in `base64encode()` does not help because the failure occurs inside `file`, before encoding; `base64encode` is for strings you already have. `filebase64sha256` returns a digest for change detection. `templatefile(path, vars)` renders a file with string-template syntax (`${ }` interpolation and `%{ }` directives), and the only variables visible inside are the keys of the `vars` object. If the template uses `${region}` and `${name}` but the call passes only `{ name = var.name }`, plan fails with an error that the vars map lacks the key, even though the module declares `var.region`. Module inputs, locals and resources are not visible unless passed in: `{ name = var.name, region = var.region }`. A wrong script thus never reaches an instance. `*.tftpl` is only a naming convention, and a template cannot call `templatefile` recursively.

examPoints: A question asking for the value of cidrsubnet or cidrhost is solved by computing block sizes (a /20 is 16 steps of 256 in the third octet), not by reusing the newbits number as the octet step.

A question where merge, try or coalesce is given nested maps or null is testing shallow replacement (merge), error-versus-null (try returns null for an existing null attribute) and null-or-empty skipping (coalesce).
A question about a failing file or templatefile call is testing text versus binary (file versus filebase64) and that templatefile sees only the keys of the vars object.

quiz.q: What does the expression `try(local.cfg.db.port, 5432)` return when `local.cfg = { db = { port = null } }`, and which expression gives 5432 in that case?
choices: It returns 5432, because try treats a null value as a failed evaluation and moves on to its fallback argument
It returns `null`, because the attribute exists and reading it is not an error; `coalesce(local.cfg.db.port, 5432)` gives 5432
It fails with an an unsupported-attribute error error, because try cannot be used on an object that holds a null attribute
It returns `null`, and `can(local.cfg.db.port)` is the expression that returns the fallback port number 5432
quiz.explain: try reacts to evaluation errors only, and a null attribute is valid, so null comes back; coalesce skips null and empty strings. Choice D is wrong because can returns a boolean, never a fallback value.

quiz.q: A module must pass a `.p12` certificate bundle to an argument as a Base64 string, and `file("${path.module}/bundle.p12")` fails with an invalid UTF-8 error. Which change fixes it?
choices: Use `filebase64("${path.module}/bundle.p12")`, which reads the raw bytes and returns them Base64-encoded
Use `base64encode(file("${path.module}/bundle.p12"))`, which encodes the text after it has been read
Use `templatefile("${path.module}/bundle.p12", {})`, which accepts binary content when no variables are passed
Rename the file with a `.tftpl` extension, because the extension decides whether Terraform reads it as binary
quiz.explain: filebase64 reads bytes directly. Choice B still calls file first, so the same failure happens before encoding, and choice D is wrong because the extension is only a naming convention.

days.recap: Predict by computing: cidrsubnet and cidrhost count addresses, merge is shallow, try catches errors but returns an existing null, coalesce skips null and empty strings. Know flatten versus concat, toset versus distinct, element wrapping, braces versus brackets with the ellipsis, and file versus filebase64 versus templatefile vars.

days.title: Advanced Configurations, Provider Configuration and the Terraform MCP Server

concepts.heading: Dynamic Blocks and Optional Object Attributes
concepts.body: Nested blocks are not arguments, so they cannot be set to `null` or switched off with `count`, which applies only to whole resources, data sources and modules. A `dynamic` block generates zero or more nested blocks from a collection, and the idiom for an optional block is `for_each = var.versioning_enabled ? [1] : []`: one element gives one block, an empty list gives none. Inside `content` you get a temporary object with `.key` and `.value`, named after the block label by default. Setting `iterator = rule` renames it, and then only `rule.key` and `rule.value` exist; keeping `ingress.value.port` produces an unknown reference. Renaming helps when nested dynamic blocks share a label. The docs advise dynamic blocks mainly to hide detail in reusable modules and to write blocks literally elsewhere. For inputs, `optional(type)` inside an object type lets the caller omit an attribute. Given `object({ name = string, port = optional(number, 8080), tls = optional(bool) })` and a caller passing `{ name = "api", port = null }`: `tls` is `null` (no default given), while `port` is `8080`, because a non-null default is substituted both when the attribute is omitted and when it is explicitly null.

concepts.heading: count Versus for_each in Real Designs
concepts.body: `count` takes a whole number and addresses instances by position (`res[0]`); it is the simple tool for zero-or-one toggles and N identical copies. `for_each` takes a map or a set of strings and addresses instances by key (`res["billing"]`), so each keeps its identity when siblings come and go. A request-driven list of similar objects, such as teams adding an entry to a `queues` map in tfvars, is the standard for_each case: `each.key` is the team name, `each.value.retention` carries the settings, and adding or removing a key creates or destroys only that instance. Both the count value and the for_each keys must be known at plan time, and a resource may use only one of the two. For a toggle, `aws_eip.nat[0].public_ip` in an output fails with an invalid index when `count = var.enable_nat ? 1 : 0` is false. Either `one(aws_eip.nat[*].public_ip)` (null for an empty list) or the conditional `var.enable_nat ? aws_eip.nat[0].public_ip : null` works, because a conditional evaluates only the chosen arm. Switching an existing resource between count and for_each, or adding either to it, changes addresses and needs `moved` blocks to avoid destroy and create.

concepts.heading: Custom Conditions in the Right Place
concepts.body: Resources and data sources accept `lifecycle { precondition { ... } postcondition { ... } }`, while an `output` block takes only a `precondition`, written directly in the block. A precondition is evaluated before the object is read or created, so it tests inputs and cannot use `self`. A postcondition is evaluated afterwards, may use `self`, and objects that depend on the checked object are not processed until it passes. A `check` block runs assertions after planning and applying; failures are warnings only. `validation` exists only on input variables. Choose by where the knowledge exists and whether the run must stop. 'Fail early with my own message when no approved AMI exists' fits a postcondition on the data source, because the result is known only after the lookup. 'Block the apply if the subnet is public' needs a blocking construct, not a check. 'Reject a bad instance type before any call' fits variable validation. An error from a condition reads far better than an obscure provider failure later in the apply, and a postcondition on a data source also stops downstream resources from using a value that is not acceptable. Used together, these constructs turn assumptions in a module into enforced rules.

concepts.heading: Provider Configuration: Inheritance, Aliases and Accounts
concepts.body: Each account or region needs its own provider configuration, selected with `alias`. A child module automatically inherits the root's default (non-aliased) configurations by name, and never inherits aliased ones implicitly. With `provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1" }` and an aliased `west` configuration, `module "network" { source = "./network" }` with no `providers` argument uses `us-east-1`. To use the alias, pass `providers = { aws = aws.west }`. A module that needs two configurations of the same provider, such as a disaster-recovery module with a primary bucket and a replica, declares extras with `configuration_aliases = [aws.replica]` inside `required_providers`, uses `provider = aws.replica` on resources, and the caller maps names through `providers`. Without the declaration Terraform rejects the module. Provider blocks inside reusable modules are discouraged since they prevent `count`, `for_each` and `depends_on` on the module and complicate cleanup. Provider arguments are ordinary expressions (`region = var.region`), though values known only after apply should be avoided; `assume_role { role_arn = ... }` lets one set of base credentials act in other accounts. `for_each` and `count` are not allowed on provider blocks, so every alias is written out. Child modules do not inherit provider sources or versions and declare `required_providers` themselves.

concepts.heading: Provider Versions, the Lock File and the Terraform MCP Server
concepts.body: `~> 5.40` allows `>= 5.40.0, < 6.0.0` (the rightmost component may increase), whereas `~> 5.40.0` allows only 5.40.x. If the lock file records 5.42.0 and 5.60.0 and 6.0.0 are released, plain `terraform init` keeps 5.42.0 while it satisfies the constraint, `terraform init -upgrade` picks 5.60.0 and rewrites the lock file, and only changing the constraint can select 6.0.0. Checksums are platform-sensitive: packages installed from a filesystem or network mirror can be verified only for the platform where init ran. When macOS arm64 developers commit the lock file and Linux amd64 CI installs from an internal mirror, the checksum error is solved durably with `terraform providers lock -platform=linux_amd64 -platform=darwin_arm64` and by committing the result; deleting the lock file or upgrading in CI gives up pinning. The Terraform MCP server lets an AI coding assistant call Terraform-specific tools through the Model Context Protocol. Registry tools such as `search_providers` and `get_provider_details` return current documentation, reducing outdated arguments. The `terraform` and `registry-private` toolsets register only with a valid `TFE_TOKEN`; destructive operations such as `action_run` stay disabled until `ENABLE_TF_OPERATIONS=true`. `--toolsets` and `--tools` cannot be combined. The default transport is stdio; streamable HTTP binds to `127.0.0.1:8080` unless `TRANSPORT_HOST` is changed, and should use TLS.

examPoints: A question about an optional nested block (not an argument) points to a dynamic block with a one-element or empty list, not count and not null.
A question where a module must use two regions or accounts is testing configuration_aliases in the module and a providers map in the caller; aliased configurations are never inherited implicitly.

A question on the Terraform MCP server asking which settings let an assistant approve runs wants a valid TFE_TOKEN (for the terraform toolset) and ENABLE_TF_OPERATIONS=true; the MCP server adds current documentation and tools, not model training.

quiz.q: A caller has `provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1" }` and `provider "aws" { alias = "west" region = "us-west-2" }`. It calls `module "network" { source = "./network" }` with no `providers` argument. Which region does the module use, and how does the caller select the alias?
choices: us-west-2, because Terraform inherits every provider configuration and the most recently declared one wins
us-east-1, because only the default configuration is inherited; the alias is passed with `providers = { aws = aws.west }`
us-east-1, because modules never inherit providers; the alias is selected with `provider = aws.west` on the module block
No region, because the module must declare its own provider block before it can create any resources
quiz.explain: A child inherits only the default non-aliased configuration; aliased ones are passed through the providers map. Choice C names an argument that the module block does not use for this purpose.

quiz.q: A team starts the Terraform MCP server with `TRANSPORT_MODE=streamable-http` on a shared build host. Requests on the host work, but colleagues' clients cannot connect to port 8080. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The server also needs `ENABLE_TF_OPERATIONS=true` before it accepts connections from any other machine on the network
The stdio transport is mandatory for shared use, so streamable HTTP must be replaced by a stdio client on every machine
The server binds to `127.0.0.1` by default, so `TRANSPORT_HOST` must be set to an interface such as `0.0.0.0`, with TLS
The `/health` endpoint is the MCP endpoint, so clients must be configured with that path instead of `/mcp`
quiz.explain: Streamable HTTP defaults to the loopback address, so remote clients need TRANSPORT_HOST changed (and TLS). Choice A is wrong because that switch only enables destructive operations.

days.recap: Optional nested blocks use dynamic with a one-or-zero list; optional() defaults replace null, count suits toggles and for_each keyed collections. Put conditions where the knowledge exists. Providers: only default configs are inherited, aliases need providers maps and configuration_aliases, the lock file needs every platform's hashes, and the MCP server gates destructive tools.

days.title: Remote Backends and Remote State: Locking, Migration and Protection

concepts.heading: S3 Backend Locking
concepts.body: Locking stops two runs from writing the same state at once, and the `s3` backend supports it only if you opt in, with two mechanisms. S3 native locking, `use_lockfile = true`, makes Terraform create a lock object named like the state key plus `.tflock` using S3 conditional writes; the object exists while a run holds the lock and is deleted afterwards. DynamoDB locking, `dynamodb_table`, names a table whose partition key is `LockID` (string); the docs mark this method deprecated and due for removal in a future minor version, and both can be set together during migration. A team that wants to retire the table and keep locking sets `use_lockfile = true` and removes `dynamodb_table`. Permissions follow the mechanism: the role needs `s3:GetObject`, `s3:PutObject` and `s3:DeleteObject` on the `.tflock` key in addition to the state key. Missing delete rights leave the lock behind, and the next run then reports a held lock. That symptom (a lock never released after a successful run) points to permissions on the lock object, not to a corrupt state. Locking serializes writers; it does not keep a copy of state, which is a different protection covered later in this day.

concepts.heading: Changing a Backend: -migrate-state Versus -reconfigure
concepts.body: Terraform remembers the initialized backend in `.terraform/`. When the backend block changes, for example a new `bucket` value, `terraform init` stops with a backend-configuration-changed error until you say what should happen to the state: `-migrate-state` or `-reconfigure` must be supplied. `terraform init -migrate-state` copies the existing state to the new backend and may prompt to confirm each workspace; `-force-copy` answers yes to those prompts and implies `-migrate-state`. `terraform init -reconfigure` ignores the previous configuration and migrates nothing, so the new location starts empty and the next plan proposes creating every resource again. That is the classic production incident: someone picks -reconfigure to silence the error, and the plan wants to build everything that already exists. Always copy `terraform.tfstate` aside first, as the docs strongly recommend. Moving from an `s3` backend to HCP Terraform follows the same path: a configuration has one state storage setting, either a `backend` block or a `cloud` block, never both. After you swap in the cloud block, init detects the previous backend and offers to copy the state into the workspace; if the cloud block uses tags, it asks which workspace name to create or use for each existing workspace.

concepts.heading: Partial Configuration for Environment-Specific Backends
concepts.body: The backend block is read before variables are evaluated, so it cannot reference `var.` values or locals. Four environments sharing one `s3` block in Git, with bucket and key that differ per environment and must not live in the repository, use partial configuration: leave the arguments out and supply them at init. Options are a file via `-backend-config=PATH` (lines of `key = "value"`), key/value pairs via `-backend-config="key=value"` (the shell history keeps these), or interactive prompts for missing values. Terraform still requires at least an empty `backend "s3" {}` in a root file, to name the backend type. Watch the leak paths: the merged configuration is written in plain text under `.terraform/` and also into plan files, which is why HashiCorp recommends environment variables for credentials rather than putting them in -backend-config. A common design is one small file per environment, such as `prod.s3.tfbackend` (the docs recommend the `*.backendname.tfbackend` naming pattern, but it is only a convention), selected by the pipeline at init. Switching between those files in the same working directory is itself a backend change, so it needs the same -migrate-state versus -reconfigure decision as above, and a clean checkout per environment avoids the confusion.

concepts.heading: The cloud Block: Name Versus Tags
concepts.body: The `cloud` block links a working directory to HCP Terraform workspaces. `workspaces { name = "..." }` ties the directory to one workspace. `workspaces { tags = [...] }` ties it to every workspace in the organization with those tags, optionally limited with `project`. The CLI then maps its own workspace commands onto them: `terraform workspace list` shows the matching workspaces, `terraform workspace select` picks one, and if no workspace has the tags, init offers to create one. `name` and `tags` cannot be combined. Each run still targets exactly one workspace, with its own state and variables. Scenario: a root module declares `cloud { organization = "acme" workspaces { tags = ["app:web"] } }` and three workspaces carry that tag; after init, `terraform workspace list` shows the three matches and `terraform workspace select` picks the one the run will target. This is a different thing from the CLI workspaces of backends such as S3, where all workspaces belong to one backend configuration and differ only in state key. Remote execution then handles state, locks and run history in the service, so a laptop is no longer the place where state lives.

concepts.heading: Backups, Versioning and Picking the Right Workspace
concepts.body: Three protections get confused. Locking (`use_lockfile`) serializes writers and holds no copy of state. Encryption (`encrypt`) protects data at rest, but an overwrite still replaces the object. Versioning keeps earlier versions of the same S3 key, and the S3 backend docs highly recommend enabling bucket versioning so state can be recovered after accidental deletion or human error. After a mistaken `terraform state push` replaced production state with an older snapshot, the bucket setting that allows restore is versioning; you restore the earlier object version and then run `terraform plan` to see what differs from the real infrastructure. The `-backup` option is a legacy option for local state files, not remote backends. A related diagnosis: a new engineer clones the repository and `terraform plan` proposes creating every resource, `terraform state list` is empty, and the backend block is unchanged. With backends that support multiple CLI workspaces each workspace has its own state under a separate key, and a fresh clone starts in `default`. Check `terraform workspace show` and `terraform workspace list`, then `terraform workspace select prod`. If the workspace is right, check bucket, key or prefix, and credentials for the correct account. Do not apply that plan, because it would create duplicates.

examPoints: A question where changing a backend argument stops init with a backend-configuration-changed error and the state must follow is answered by -migrate-state; -reconfigure leaves the new location empty and the next plan wants to create everything.
A question about retiring DynamoDB locking points to use_lockfile = true and delete permissions on the .tflock key; locking and versioning protect against different failures.
A question where a fresh clone plans to create everything with an empty state list is a workspace or backend-argument diagnosis, not drift: check the selected workspace before anything else.

quiz.q: An engineer changes the `bucket` value in the `s3` backend block to a new bucket and runs `terraform init`, which stops with a backend-configuration-changed error. The existing state must be available in the new bucket. Which command does this?
choices: `terraform init -reconfigure`, which copies the state into the new bucket and then updates the saved backend settings
`terraform init -migrate-state`, which copies the existing state to the new backend after the state is backed up
`terraform state push` with no arguments, which sends the state to the bucket that is named in the new block
`terraform apply -refresh-only`, which recreates the state in whichever bucket the configuration names now
quiz.explain: -migrate-state copies state to the new backend. Choice A is the trap: -reconfigure ignores the old configuration and migrates nothing, so the next plan would propose creating every resource.

quiz.q: A shared state bucket for production is written by a pipeline. A mistaken `terraform state push` replaced the production state with an older snapshot. Which bucket setting lets the team restore the previous snapshot?
choices: Native locking with `use_lockfile`, because the lock object keeps a copy of the state that preceded each write
Server-side encryption with `encrypt`, because encrypted objects cannot be overwritten by a later state push
The `-backup` option of the CLI, because it stores a timestamped copy of every remote state automatically
Bucket versioning, because earlier versions of the same state key are kept and an older version can be restored
quiz.explain: Versioning keeps previous object versions; after restoring one, run a plan to see the difference from reality. Choice A confuses serialization of writers with backup, and -backup applies to local state files.

days.recap: Opt in to locking with use_lockfile (DynamoDB is deprecated); changing a backend needs -migrate-state, because -reconfigure copies nothing. Use partial configuration for per-environment values, know cloud block name versus tags, and rely on bucket versioning for recovery. An empty state after a clone usually means the wrong workspace.

days.title: Drift, moved and removed Blocks, and Dependency Chains

concepts.heading: Drift: What a Normal Plan Shows
concepts.body: Drift is real infrastructure differing from what state records. A normal plan first refreshes state by reading each tracked object from the provider. If an operator terminated `aws_instance.web` in the console, the provider reports it as not found, and Terraform drops it from the in-memory state before comparing. The plan lists it under 'Objects have changed outside of Terraform', so reviewers see the drift. Because the configuration still declares the resource and the refreshed state has none, the plan proposes a create, not a replacement, and nothing changes until apply. `terraform apply -refresh-only` would instead record the deletion in state without recreating anything. The reverse case, an object edited in place, appears as an in-place update back to the configured value. Remediation is therefore a decision between two directions: let code win (a normal apply restores the configured value) or accept reality (a refresh-only apply updates state, and you then edit the code to match). Read the drift section of the plan before deciding, because applying blindly after a deletion creates a new object with a new ID and anything that held the old ID, such as a DNS record outside Terraform, must be updated.

concepts.heading: Detecting Drift Early
concepts.body: To catch out-of-band changes to production without applying anything, use a command that reads the remote objects. `terraform plan -refresh-only` compares state against real objects and proposes only state changes. With `-detailed-exitcode`, the exit code is 0 for no changes, 2 when changes exist and 1 for an error, which suits a scheduled job that alerts on 2. Saving the refresh-only plan with `-out` and reading it with `terraform show -json` exposes a `resource_drift` list that a script can inspect. Commands that do not detect drift are worth naming: `terraform validate` checks syntax and internal consistency offline, `terraform fmt` checks style, and `terraform state list` only prints addresses already in state. None of them contacts the provider to compare. Distinguish the three tools for acting on drift. A normal plan and apply will revert drift towards the configuration. A refresh-only plan and apply accepts reality into state and changes no infrastructure. A targeted replace, `-replace=ADDRESS`, is for an object that is broken but still present. Choose by which side is correct, not by which command is shortest.

concepts.heading: moved Blocks: Refactor Without Destroying
concepts.body: State tracks an instance by its full address. Rename a resource block, add `count` or `for_each` to a resource, or rename a for_each key, and the old address has no configuration while the new address has no state; Terraform does not guess, so the plan destroys one and creates the other. A `moved` block records the mapping in code: `moved { from = aws_instance.web  to = aws_instance.web[0] }`. On the next plan the object is shown as moved, and only genuinely new instances are created. Adding `count = 2` to a block with an existing single instance is the typical case: the move keeps the original as the first instance and only the second is created. The same applies when switching between count and for_each. A module used by 30 workspaces that renames `aws_s3_bucket.logs` to `aws_s3_bucket.audit` should ship `moved { from = aws_s3_bucket.logs to = aws_s3_bucket.audit }` inside the module: each workspace with state at the old address retargets it at its next plan, with no infrastructure change, and consumers receive the move as they upgrade. `terraform state mv` does the same by hand but once per state, unreviewed, which is error-prone across 30 workspaces. Keep the block long enough for every consumer to apply once.

concepts.heading: removed Blocks and state rm: Stop Managing Without Destroying
concepts.body: A resource that is in state but no longer in configuration is planned for destroy. If a team deletes the `aws_db_instance.legacy` block but wants the database to keep running, state the intent in code with a `removed` block: `removed { from = aws_db_instance.legacy  lifecycle { destroy = false } }`. Terraform drops the object from state and leaves the real database alone. `destroy = true`, the default, would destroy it, which is the same as simply deleting the block. The block is reviewed in the plan and travels with the code. `terraform state rm ADDRESS` is the one-off command version: it deletes the binding between an address and its real object in state and never calls the provider to delete anything, so the object keeps running. If the configuration still contains the block after `state rm`, the plan shows a create, and applying it builds a second instance while the first becomes unmanaged, still costing money or holding a name or IP. The correct combinations are therefore: remove the resource block as well (or use a removed block) to stop managing, and use `import` to adopt the object again. Never run `state rm` and leave the code unchanged.

concepts.heading: Dependency Chains: Edges, Destroy Order and Cross-State Links
concepts.body: Terraform builds a directed graph of resources and data sources and walks it so independent nodes run in parallel (default parallelism is 10 operations) and dependent ones wait. An implicit edge comes from referencing another object's attribute, such as `aws_subnet.a.id`; an explicit edge comes from `depends_on`, meant for hidden dependencies where no attribute is referenced, for example an instance whose boot script needs an IAM policy to be attached. File position never matters, since all `.tf` files in a directory load as one module, and a shared local creates a reference to the local, not an ordering between the two resources. `terraform graph` prints the simplified graph in Graphviz DOT format (`terraform graph | dot -Tsvg > graph.svg`), which is how you see ripple effects before refactoring a shared networking module. Destruction walks edges in the opposite direction: with `depends_on = [aws_iam_role_policy.boot]` on an instance, creation is policy then instance, and destroy is instance then policy. Cross-state dependencies are invisible in the producer's graph. `terraform_remote_state` reads root-module outputs of another configuration, so renaming `vpc_id` to `network_id` breaks twelve consumer workspaces on their next plan. Publish the new output alongside the old, update and apply the consumers, and only then remove the old output.

examPoints: A question where a resource was deleted in the console and the plan wants to create it tests drift handling: the plan shows a create, and refresh-only would record the deletion without recreating.

A question about renaming a resource or adding count with no infrastructure change wants a moved block (reviewable, ships with a module); stopping management without destroying wants a removed block with destroy = false.
A question about changing a root output used by other workspaces is a cross-state dependency: add the new output, migrate consumers, then remove the old one.

quiz.q: A team deletes the block for `aws_db_instance.legacy` and wants Terraform to forget the database while it keeps running. The plan currently shows a destroy. What is the correct change?
choices: Add `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` to the deleted block so that Terraform keeps the database during the apply
Run `terraform apply -refresh-only` so that state records the database as deleted while the real database keeps running
Add a `removed` block for the address with `lifecycle { destroy = false }`, so Terraform drops it from state only
Add a `moved` block from the old address to a new address, which lets Terraform skip all work for that database
quiz.explain: A removed block with destroy = false stops management without destroying the object. Choice A cannot work because the resource block is gone, and a refresh-only apply would not change what the configuration plans.

quiz.q: An engineer runs `terraform state rm aws_instance.app` for a tracked instance, but the `aws_instance.app` block remains in the configuration. What does the next plan show?
choices: A destroy of the running instance, because state rm marks the object for removal at the next apply
No changes, because state rm only hides the address and the configuration still matches the real object
A create of a new instance, and applying it would leave the first instance running but unmanaged
An error, because state rm is blocked while the matching resource block still exists in the configuration
quiz.explain: state rm only deletes the address-to-object binding and never calls the provider, so configuration with no state plans a create. Choice A is the opposite of what happens: nothing is destroyed.

days.recap: Drift shows in a normal plan as objects changed outside Terraform; refresh-only with -detailed-exitcode detects it without changing infrastructure. Moved blocks refactor addresses, removed blocks with destroy = false stop management, state rm leaves the object running. Dependencies come from references and depends_on, destroy runs in reverse, and output renames break remote_state consumers.

days.title: Upgrading Terraform Versions and Inspecting State

concepts.heading: required_version and the Forward-Only State
concepts.body: `required_version` in the `terraform` block states which CLI versions may use the configuration; if the running CLI does not match, Terraform stops with an unsupported-Terraform-version error. The block accepts constants only. To allow 1.14 and 1.15 but reject any 2.x, `~> 1.12` means `>= 1.12.0, < 2.0.0`; `~> 1.12.0` allows only patch releases (`< 1.13.0`); `>= 1.12` has no upper bound and accepts 2.x; `= 1.14.0` allows exactly one version. Terraform records the CLI version that last wrote state. Within v1.x the compatibility promise lets you upgrade from any v1.x to any later v1.x, but downgrading is not guaranteed, because later releases may introduce new storage formats for state snapshots that earlier versions cannot read. So when a developer applies with a newer CLI and a teammate on an older one gets an error that the state was written by a newer version, the way forward is to move everyone to the newer CLI and put the minimum in `required_version` so mismatches fail early and clearly. Do not hand-edit version fields in the state; that bypasses a protection which stops an old CLI from corrupting data it does not understand.

concepts.heading: Rolling a CLI Upgrade Through Environments
concepts.body: A company running dev, staging and prod from one configuration and moving from Terraform 1.12 to 1.15 has two supported practices. First, go lowest-risk environment first: run `terraform plan` with the new CLI against dev, where a healthy upgrade shows no unexpected changes, then staging, then prod. Second, read the release notes and upgrade guides for deprecations and behavior changes, and set `required_version` so older CLIs stop early. Skipping minors within v1.x is supported, so you do not need to apply every release in turn. Remember the one-way nature of state: once the new CLI has applied, the old CLI may not read the state, so rolling back after an apply is not guaranteed; the plan-only trial in dev is what makes the rollout safe. `terraform init -upgrade` updates providers and modules within their constraints and never installs the Terraform CLI, so it is not an upgrade step for Terraform itself. Treat the CLI upgrade as its own change, with the pipeline image or version pinned in one place, and watch for plans that show changes nobody wrote; those usually point to a behavior change that needs reading, not to drift.

concepts.heading: CLI and Providers Upgrade Independently
concepts.body: Terraform core and providers are separate programs with separate versions. Upgrading the CLI does not change which provider releases are selected. The dependency lock file `.terraform.lock.hcl` records each selected provider version and checksums, and `terraform init` reuses them as long as they still satisfy the `required_providers` constraints; only `terraform init -upgrade` moves to newer ones. A team that wants no provider changes in the CLI rollout therefore commits the lock file so every environment and CI job installs identical providers, and then upgrades providers as a second, separate change, which makes a surprising plan easier to attribute. Before a provider major upgrade across a root module and its child modules, `terraform providers` prints a tree of the requirements of the root module, then each child module, then the providers state tracks, and it shows which module blocks a newer provider version. `terraform version` shows installed versions but not per-module constraints. After changing constraints, run `terraform init -upgrade` to select versions and rewrite the lock file. Very old state may carry the legacy provider address `registry.terraform.io/-/aws`; `terraform state replace-provider FROM TO` rewrites the provider recorded for every resource, asks for confirmation and writes under the lock on a remote backend. `providers lock` only writes hashes and `state mv` moves resource addresses.

concepts.heading: Choosing the Inspection Command
concepts.body: `terraform state list [address...]` prints the address of every resource instance in state, one per line, and given an address it filters: `module.network` returns only entries within that module, which is quick on a state of 400 addresses. `-id=ID` filters by a real object's ID. `terraform state show ADDRESS` prints the attributes of one resource instance as readable text and does not accept a whole module. Keyed instances need exact quoting: the address is `aws_instance.web["a"]`, and in a Linux shell the double quotes are stripped unless the whole address is in single quotes, which yields an invalid `aws_instance.web[a]`; copy the exact address from state list. For `count`, the form is `aws_instance.web[0]`, and dot notation is for attributes and module paths, not instance keys. `terraform show` prints the whole state or a saved plan in human form, and `terraform show -json` gives a documented, stable JSON representation meant for tools, which a compliance script should filter with `jq`. `terraform state pull` prints the raw state file, whose format is internal and may change between versions. `terraform output` reads root outputs only, and `terraform graph` prints DOT with no address filter.

concepts.heading: Sensitive Data, Output Flags and State Selection
concepts.body: State maps addresses to real objects and stores each object's attributes, including ones a provider returns that are secret: initial passwords, generated keys, connection strings. `sensitive = true` hides values from Terraform's CLI output; it does not encrypt or redact the state document. Given `output "db_password" { value = random_password.db.result sensitive = true }`, plain `terraform output db_password` prints `<sensitive>`, whereas `terraform output -raw db_password` prints the string with no quotes or formatting, handy in scripts, and `-json` prints JSON. The docs state that -json and -raw display sensitive values in plain text, so the shell, CI logs and state access need care. `terraform state pull` downloads the latest state from the backend and prints raw JSON, useful with `jq`; it is a read operation, while `state push` is a separate risky overwrite that most teams restrict. Auditors asking how state is protected get the real answer: restrict bucket or workspace access, enable encryption at rest and log reads. The final inspection skill is diagnosis: when `state list` prints nothing for a repository that has production resources, suspect the selected workspace or backend arguments before suspecting drift.

examPoints: A question asking for a constraint that allows later 1.x releases but rejects 2.x wants ~> 1.12 (or similar); ~> 1.12.0 allows patch releases only, and required_version never installs a CLI.
A question where an older CLI cannot read state tells you state is forward-only within v1.x: upgrade everyone and raise the minimum in required_version, never edit state versions by hand.
A question asking for machine-readable full state wants terraform show -json; list gives addresses, state show one instance, and -raw or -json output reveals sensitive values.

quiz.q: A team upgrades the CLI from 1.12 to 1.15 and wants no provider changes in the same rollout. After the upgrade, `terraform init` runs in CI. What keeps provider versions the same?
choices: The committed `.terraform.lock.hcl`, because init reuses the recorded versions while they satisfy the constraints
The new CLI itself, because every Terraform release pins the provider versions that were current at its release
The `required_version` constraint, because it also limits the provider versions that init is allowed to install
Running `terraform init -upgrade` in CI, because it keeps the versions that are already installed on the runner
quiz.explain: Providers and the CLI version independently, and the lock file holds the selected provider versions and checksums. Choice D is the reverse: -upgrade moves to the newest allowed versions and rewrites the lock file.

quiz.q: A compliance script needs every resource attribute in the current state as machine-readable JSON, to filter with `jq`. Which command fits best, and what must be kept in mind about its output?
choices: `terraform state list`, which prints JSON for every resource and omits secret attribute values
`terraform state show` without an address, which prints the whole state as a single JSON document
`terraform output -json`, which prints every resource attribute in the state with sensitive values redacted
`terraform show -json`, a documented format meant for tools; it includes attribute values, so treat it as sensitive
quiz.explain: show -json is the stable machine format and contains values. Choice A is wrong because state list prints addresses only, and choice C is wrong because -json outputs display sensitive values in plain text.

days.recap: Constrain the CLI with required_version, upgrade lowest-risk environment first and remember state is forward-only within v1.x. CLI and providers move separately (lock file, terraform providers, state replace-provider). Pick state list, state show, show -json or pull deliberately, and treat -raw, -json and state pull as secret-bearing.

days.title: Scaling Projects, Plan Modes and Applying Safely

concepts.heading: Why and How to Split a Large Project
concepts.body: A configuration and its state are one unit: every plan refreshes every object in the state, and every apply can touch any of them. A root module with networking, a database tier and dozens of services therefore has slow plans and a large blast radius, because a typo in a service change can sit in the same plan as the database. Raising `-parallelism` does not help much, since the docs say Terraform does not use it to handle API rate limits. The recommended fix is several smaller configurations, each with its own state, split along ownership (network team, platform team, app team) and change frequency (foundation rarely, services daily). A separate state also means a separate lock, access policy and apply history. The price is coupling work: producers must be applied before consumers, and values move through outputs or data sources. Routine `-target` is not the answer; the docs reserve it for exceptional cases, and it leaves the state out of step with the configuration. Splitting is a governance and runtime decision, not a file-layout one: repeated module calls with different names or `for_each` keys coexist happily in one state.

concepts.heading: Sharing Values Between States
concepts.body: After a split, configuration B often needs an object from configuration A. `terraform_remote_state` reads the latest state snapshot from A's backend and returns only A's root module outputs. Three practical rules follow. First, only root outputs are visible: an output of `module.vpc` reaches consumers only if the root re-exports it with its own `output` block, and the producer must be applied after that output is added or the consumer fails with output not found. Second, the reader needs access to the whole state snapshot, which often holds secrets, so a security reviewer is right to object. Third, with the S3 backend the data source's `workspace` argument defaults to the producer's default workspace, so a `prod` consumer silently receives dev data unless it sets `workspace = terraform.workspace` or points at a different key. Narrower alternatives are a key/value store or DNS record published by A and read with a matching data source, or tags looked up with a provider data source. The `defaults` argument supplies fallback outputs when the state is empty, which helps bootstrap but can mask a missing apply.

concepts.heading: Plan Modes and Options
concepts.body: Plan has three modes: normal (reconcile with the configuration), `-destroy` (plan removal of every managed object) and `-refresh-only` (plan to update state and root outputs with real values, changing no resource). Options adjust a mode. `-replace=ADDRESS` plans a replacement of one instance even when nothing differs, which is how you rebuild a corrupted but healthy-looking server; it succeeds `terraform taint` and cannot be combined with `-destroy`. `-refresh-only` is the answer when someone resized a database in the console and you want the state to record it: afterwards, the next normal plan will still propose reverting it unless the code is updated too. `-refresh=false` skips the read of real objects, which is faster and gentler on throttled APIs but means out-of-band changes are missing from the plan. `-target` narrows the scope and is for exceptional recovery only. `-detailed-exitcode` changes the status: 0 no changes, 1 error, 2 changes present, so a script treating every non-zero as failure will break on pending changes.

concepts.heading: Saved Plans and Their Rules
concepts.body: `terraform plan -out=tfplan` writes an opaque file with the full configuration, all planned values and all plan options, including input variables. Sensitive values are stored in cleartext even though the terminal hides them, so the artifact needs restricted access. Inspect it with `terraform show tfplan` or `-json`. Do not give it a `.tf` suffix, or Terraform tries to read it as configuration. Applying a saved plan is itself the approval: there is no prompt and `-auto-approve` is ignored. Because the file already holds the final decisions, Terraform rejects extra planning options such as `-var` on `terraform apply tfplan`; to change a value, plan again and review again. A saved plan records the state it was computed against. If another pipeline changed that state in between, apply fails with a stale plan error, and the fix is to re-plan, re-review and apply. A state lock is released between separate plan and apply jobs, so serialize runs per state in the CI system instead of relying on locking alone. The apply machine also needs the same providers (init with the same lock file) and Terraform version.

concepts.heading: Partial Failures and Tainted Objects
concepts.body: Terraform has no transactions and no rollback. State is written as the apply proceeds, so if 30 resources are planned and the 13th fails with an API error, the 12 that finished are recorded in state; independent operations already running normally complete, and dependents of the failed resource are not attempted. Read the error, fix the cause (permissions, quota, an invalid argument) and run plan again: it compares the configuration with the updated state and shows only the unfinished work, so rerunning is the recovery, not a manual cleanup. A resource whose creation failed after the remote object was partly built, for example because a provisioner failed, is saved as tainted. A tainted object is considered degraded, and the next plan proposes to replace it (destroy then create, or create then destroy with `create_before_destroy`). `terraform plan -replace=ADDRESS` gives the same result on demand, and `terraform untaint` marks an object healthy again once you have verified it. Never disable locking with `-lock=false` to get past errors during recovery.

examPoints: A question about a slow plan or a typo that reached the database is testing state boundaries: split by ownership and change frequency with separate states, not routine -target, higher -parallelism or CLI workspaces.
A question where a saved plan fails or is rejected is testing its rules: a stale plan after other state changes needs a new plan and review, and -var cannot be added to terraform apply tfplan.
A question about a pipeline that fails whenever changes exist is testing -detailed-exitcode, where exit code 2 means success with changes and 1 means error.

quiz.q: A console edit shrank a managed database. The team wants state to record the new size now, without touching infrastructure, and then decide about the code. Which command does that, and what will the next normal plan show if the code still has the old size?
choices: terraform plan -replace on the database; the next plan is empty because the new instance matches the code
terraform apply -refresh-only; the next plan proposes changing the database back to the size in the code
terraform plan -refresh=false; the next plan proposes nothing because the console size is accepted
terraform apply -target on the database; the next plan keeps the console size because -target updates the code
quiz.explain: Refresh-only updates state and outputs with real values and changes no resource, so the next normal plan compares the unchanged code with the new state and proposes to revert. Choice A rebuilds the database, C only skips reading real objects, and D narrows scope but never edits code.

quiz.q: A pipeline applies a reviewed file with `terraform apply -var="size=large" tfplan` and fails. A second pipeline had applied a change to the same state after the plan was made. What are the two problems?
choices: The file needs a .tf suffix, and -auto-approve is missing so the apply waits for a prompt
The plan is stale because the state changed, and a saved plan cannot take extra -var options
Locking was disabled for the plan, and the variable size is not declared in the saved file
The state moved to a new workspace, and the plan file must be regenerated with -destroy
quiz.explain: A saved plan fixes all planning options and variables, so -var is rejected, and Terraform refuses a plan computed against an older state. Choice A is wrong because a .tf suffix breaks the file and passing the plan counts as approval; C and D invent causes.

days.recap: Split by ownership and change rate into separate states; share root outputs only (workspace argument matters). Plan: -replace rebuilds, -refresh-only fixes state, -detailed-exitcode 2 means changes. Saved plans hold cleartext secrets, go stale, accept no extra options. Failed applies keep progress; re-plan, tainted means replace.

days.title: Import, Generated Configuration and Lifecycle Rules

concepts.heading: Declarative Import with import Blocks
concepts.body: An `import` block adopts an existing object into state as part of the normal workflow. It has `to` (the resource instance address) and `id` (the provider's ID string), plus optional `for_each` and `provider`. The `to` address must match a `resource` block unless configuration is generated. Because the block is evaluated during `terraform plan`, each import appears as `to import` in the plan, so fifty existing buckets can be reviewed in a pull request before anything is applied; `terraform apply` then records them. The older CLI command `terraform import ADDRESS ID` writes state immediately with no plan, no approval and no CI visibility, and also needs a resource block. Blocks may stay in version control as a record or be removed after the apply. The `id` must be known during planning: `id = aws_instance.base.id` for an instance created in the same apply is an error, because the import is planned before anything is created. Take the ID from variables, locals or data sources, or create the dependency in an earlier run. If `to` has no matching resource block and nothing generates one, plan fails and state is unchanged.

concepts.heading: Many Objects at Once and Reading the Next Plan
concepts.body: For resources created with `for_each`, one `import` block can adopt all of them. The block accepts `for_each` as a map or a set of strings, and `each.key` and `each.value` work inside `to` and `id`: `import { for_each = toset(var.names) to = aws_s3_bucket.b[each.key] id = each.value }`. The `to` must name the specific instance, here `aws_s3_bucket.b["logs"]`; `count` is not an argument of `import`. Import records state, it does not write your `.tf` files. After the apply, a plan that shows an in-place update to several arguments means the resource block disagrees with the real object, so the apply would change the object to match the code. Decide per argument whether to edit the code to reflect reality or accept the change, and iterate until the plan shows no changes. `terraform plan -generate-config-out=PATH` can draft resource blocks for import blocks that have none, writing a new file (an existing file is an error). The docs flag it as experimental, so treat its output as a draft to review and tidy, and do not build a process around it.

concepts.heading: Moving an Object Between States
concepts.body: A real object belongs to exactly one state entry. Moving a shared VPC out of a monolith into a new network configuration without destroying it means two steps in a fixed order: make the destination adopt the object, then make the source forget it. Adopt with an `import` block and a matching `resource` block in the new configuration. Forget in the old one with a `removed` block containing `lifecycle { destroy = false }`, or with `terraform state rm`. Simply deleting the resource block from the old configuration would plan a destroy, which is the trap. Import first, then remove, so the object always has an owner and the two states never both plan changes to it. The same idea answers a team that retires a resource from management but keeps it running. Afterwards the consumers of the old output must be repointed, which is another reason to apply producers before consumers. A saved plan or a lock held by another pipeline is not involved here; the mistake to avoid is two states claiming one object, because both would try to update or delete it.

concepts.heading: create_before_destroy and prevent_destroy
concepts.body: By default a forced replacement destroys the old object and then creates the new one. `create_before_destroy = true` reverses this for zero downtime, provided both objects can exist at once, so a fixed unique `name = "web-sg"` makes the replacement fail; use `name_prefix` or a generated suffix. Terraform propagates the ordering to dependencies: if A has it and depends on B, B implicitly gets it and the state records that, which is why you cannot set it to false on B (a cycle would result). It is the only lifecycle rule stored in state. A destroy-time provisioner does not run when `create_before_destroy` is set, so cleanup that relies on it silently never happens. `prevent_destroy = true` makes any plan that would destroy the object fail, including a replacement and `terraform destroy`. It is read from the configuration, so deleting the whole resource block deletes the rule too, and Terraform then plans a normal destroy. Use a `removed` block with `destroy = false` to retire a protected object safely, and use prevent_destroy sparingly because it makes some changes impossible to apply.

concepts.heading: ignore_changes and replace_triggered_by
concepts.body: `ignore_changes` lists attributes that Terraform ignores when planning updates after creation. It lets Terraform share an object with another process: if an autoscaler changes `desired_count`, `ignore_changes = [desired_count]` stops every plan from resetting it while other arguments stay managed. Only attributes defined by the resource type can be listed, not meta-arguments or lifecycle itself. The keyword `all` ignores every attribute, so Terraform can create and destroy the object but never plans updates. `replace_triggered_by` replaces a resource when a referenced resource, instance or attribute changes. The decision rests on planned actions of managed resources, so a local value or input variable cannot be listed. To rebuild a VM whenever `var.config_version` changes, store the variable in a `terraform_data` resource (`input = var.config_version`) and reference `terraform_data.version` in `replace_triggered_by`. A reference to a resource with several instances triggers if any instance is updated or replaced. Contrast the tools: `-replace` is a one-off on the command line, `replace_triggered_by` is a standing rule in code, and taint state comes from failed creation.

examPoints: A question that adopts many existing objects while a reviewer must see them first is testing import blocks (shown in plan, support for_each) over the terraform import command, which changes state immediately.
A question where deleting a resource block still destroys a protected database is testing that prevent_destroy lives in configuration, so removal needs a removed block with destroy = false.
A question about triggering a rebuild from a variable is testing that replace_triggered_by accepts only managed resources, so the value goes through a terraform_data resource.

quiz.q: A team applies an import block with `id = aws_instance.base.id`, but that instance is created in the same configuration during the same apply. What does terraform plan report?
choices: An error, because the id of an import block must be known during the plan operation
A plan that creates the instance first and then imports it in the same apply
A warning only, and the import is skipped until the next apply
A plan that replaces the instance so the id becomes known
