quiz.explain: Import is planned before anything is created, so unknown ids are rejected. Choice B is tempting because Terraform orders dependencies, but import ids are needed at plan time. C and D describe behavior the docs do not support.

quiz.q: An engineer deletes a database's whole resource block, which had `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }`, and applies. What happens?
choices: Apply fails, because prevent_destroy is stored in state and still protects the database
Apply asks for the word destroy to be typed before continuing
Terraform destroys the database, because the rule was read from the configuration and left with the block
Terraform keeps the database and only removes it from state automatically
quiz.explain: Except for create_before_destroy, lifecycle rules are not kept in state, so removing the block removes the protection and plans a normal destroy. Use a removed block with destroy = false to stop managing it without deleting it.

days.recap: Import blocks show in plan, accept for_each (to = addr[each.key]), need ids known at plan time; the CLI command skips review. Move ownership by import first, then removed/state rm. create_before_destroy needs distinct names, prevent_destroy dies with its block, ignore_changes shares attributes, replace_triggered_by needs managed resources.

days.title: Multiple Environments and Troubleshooting Failed Runs

concepts.heading: Workspaces Versus One Root per Environment
concepts.body: A CLI workspace is a separate state instance inside the same working directory and backend; the docs describe it as technically equivalent to renaming the state file. Selecting a workspace changes only which state Terraform reads and writes, while the configuration, backend settings and credentials stay the same. That makes workspaces a poor isolation mechanism: auditors who find that dev credentials can run `terraform workspace select prod` and apply have found a design flaw, not a mistake. The docs name where workspaces fit: a parallel, throwaway copy of the infrastructure to test a change, often one workspace per feature branch, destroyed afterwards. For stages or teams that need separate credentials and access controls, the documented alternative is one small root module per environment (dev, stage, prod directories), each with its own backend and a few `module` blocks that instantiate shared modules. Costs are real: each directory has its own plugin and module cache, and updates from version control must be applied to each. Separate roots also let each environment pin its own module version, which is how a release is promoted from dev to prod.

concepts.heading: Keeping Environments Safe in Code
concepts.body: Two traps recur. First, nothing ties a variable file to a workspace. A pipeline that runs `terraform workspace select dev` and then `terraform plan -var-file=prod.tfvars` plans production sizes against dev state without any error. Guardrails: derive environment values from `terraform.workspace` in the root module (for example a map keyed by workspace name), use a directory per environment so the variable file and backend live together, or make the pipeline fail when the selected workspace and the variable file disagree. Second, `terraform.workspace` has the same value for every module call in a run. A shared module that names a bucket `"${terraform.workspace}-logs"` cannot be called twice, because the second call collides with the first and apply fails with a name that already exists. The references documentation warns such context values hurt module composability. The fix is an input such as `name_prefix`, with the root module computing each value (`"${terraform.workspace}-audit"`, `"${terraform.workspace}-access"`). Modules stay reusable, and only the root knows about environments.

concepts.heading: State Locks, Timeouts and Logs
concepts.body: Terraform locks state for every operation that can write it. A CI job killed in the middle of apply cannot release the lock, so the next run fails with Error acquiring the state lock and prints a lock ID and the holder's metadata. After confirming the earlier run is really dead, release it with `terraform force-unlock LOCK_ID`; the ID acts as a nonce so you unlock the right lock. Unlocking a lock another live run holds can create two writers, and `-lock=false` is not recommended because concurrent writers can corrupt state. When two healthy pipelines collide, the second fails at once because the default `-lock-timeout` is `0s`; add `-lock-timeout=10m` so it retries until the duration passes, ideally with a CI concurrency group that serializes runs. For diagnosis, `TF_LOG` turns on logging and sets the level (`TRACE` most verbose, then `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARN`, `ERROR`) and writes to stderr. `TF_LOG_CORE` and `TF_LOG_PROVIDER` enable core and provider logs separately, so `TF_LOG_PROVIDER=DEBUG` investigates a failing API call without core noise. `TF_LOG_PATH` appends to a file but produces nothing unless `TF_LOG` is also set.

concepts.heading: Cycle Errors and Dependency Graph Problems
concepts.body: Terraform builds a dependency graph from references and `depends_on` and checks it for cycles before walking it. A plan that stops with Error: Cycle: aws_security_group.a, aws_security_group.b usually means two objects reference each other, the classic case being inline `ingress` blocks where each group uses the other's ID. Neither can be created first. `terraform graph -type=plan -draw-cycles` highlights the cycle edges (`-draw-cycles` works with an explicit `-type`). The fix is to break the loop by moving the part that creates the second edge into its own resource: define the rules as separate rule resources that depend on both groups, while the groups depend on nothing in each other. Adding `depends_on` cannot fix a cycle because it only adds edges. The same reasoning explains why you cannot set `create_before_destroy` to false on a dependency of a resource that has it. Remember the `-parallelism` setting, default 10 graph nodes at once on plan, apply and destroy, controls how many nodes run concurrently; the docs call it an advanced option and note providers such as AWS already back off and retry on rate limits.

concepts.heading: Validate Versus Plan and Missing Variables
concepts.body: Not every failure appears at the same stage. `terraform validate` checks syntax and internal consistency (attribute names, value types, references) regardless of variables or state, and it does not contact providers or remote services. It needs an initialized directory, and `terraform init -backend=false` prepares one without touching the backend. So a pipeline whose validate stage passes can still fail at plan with a provider authentication error, or with an instance size that has the right type but that no API accepts. Plan runs with a workspace, variable values and real credentials, includes an implied validation, and talks to the APIs while refreshing and reading data. Move such errors earlier with variable `validation` blocks or preconditions. Another common automation failure: `terraform plan -input=false` reports No value for required variable. A variable without a default needs a value from `-var`, `-var-file`, `terraform.tfvars`, `*.auto.tfvars`, a `TF_VAR_<name>` environment variable or HCP Terraform. A plain `prod.tfvars` is not loaded automatically, so either pass `-var-file=prod.tfvars` or export `TF_VAR_<name>`.

examPoints: A question where dev credentials can apply to prod is testing that CLI workspaces share one backend and credentials, so separate access needs a root module and backend per environment.

A question about a lock error after a cancelled job is testing that you confirm the holder is gone and run terraform force-unlock with the lock ID, while a lock collision between live runs calls for -lock-timeout.
A question where validate passes but plan fails is testing that validate never contacts providers or remote services.

quiz.q: A shared module names a bucket `"${terraform.workspace}-logs"`. A root module calls it twice as module.audit and module.access, and the second apply fails because the bucket name already exists. What is the correct fix?
choices: Run each module call in its own CLI workspace so the workspace names differ
Add depends_on from module.access to module.audit so they are created in order
Pass a name_prefix input from the root, using terraform.workspace only in the root module
Set create_before_destroy on the bucket so the names no longer collide
quiz.explain: terraform.workspace is identical for every module call in a run, so a name built from it alone collides. Choices A and B do not change the computed name, and D affects replacement order, not naming.

quiz.q: Two healthy pipelines apply to the same state. The second always fails immediately with a lock error although the first finishes within minutes. What makes the second wait?
choices: terraform force-unlock before each run
-lock=false on the second pipeline
TF_LOG_PATH set to a shared file
-lock-timeout=10m on plan and apply
quiz.explain: The default lock timeout is 0s, so Terraform fails at once; a duration makes it retry. Choice A could release a lock a live run holds, B risks corrupting state with two writers, and C only affects logging.

days.recap: Workspaces share backend and credentials; use a root and backend per environment for separation, and pass names into modules instead of terraform.workspace. Dead job: verify, force-unlock; live collision: -lock-timeout. TF_LOG needed for TF_LOG_PATH. Cycles: split resources. validate never calls APIs.

days.title: Passing Data Between Configurations and Managing Provider and Module Versions

concepts.heading: Reading Outputs in Scripts
concepts.body: Outputs leave a configuration in three ways: the human display, `terraform output`, and the state snapshot read by other configurations. In scripts, pick the format by data shape. The default display is HCL-like and shows sensitive values as `<sensitive>`. `-json` prints a JSON object with one key per output, or just the named output, and suits `jq`. `-raw` prints one value as a plain string with no formatting and supports only string, number and boolean, so `terraform output -raw subnet_ids` on a `list(string)` fails; use `terraform output -json subnet_ids` and parse it. Both `-json` and `-raw` print sensitive values in plain text, so treat the script log as sensitive. `-no-color` does not change the data shape, and `-state` is a legacy option for the local backend. Remember that marking an output `sensitive` only redacts display; the value remains in state, which is why anyone who can read a producer's state through `terraform_remote_state` can read far more than the one output they asked for. Outputs also need to be applied before they exist: adding an output in code does not put it into state until an apply.

concepts.heading: Remote State Versus tfe_outputs
concepts.body: Inside HCP Terraform you have two ways to read another workspace's outputs. `terraform_remote_state` reads the whole state snapshot and is governed by remote state sharing settings: new workspaces do not allow other workspaces to read their state by default, and the docs advise enabling access only between workspaces that need each other. The `tfe_outputs` data source from the tfe provider returns only output values, and the docs recommend it because it does not require full access to workspace state; remote state sharing controls do not apply to it. It still needs a tfe provider token with permission on the producing workspace, so an unshared workspace such as `vpc-prod` is readable through `tfe_outputs` only if that token may access it. When you are outside HCP Terraform, the documented alternatives avoid exposing state: a key/value or object store written with a resource and read with the matching data source (for example `consul_key_prefix` or `aws_s3_object`), or a DNS record with a predictable name resolved by a DNS data source. Choose by coupling: remote state is the tightest and needs no publishing step, the others add a step but narrow who can see what.

concepts.heading: Variable Precedence as a Diagnostic Tool
concepts.body: Predicting which value wins is a frequent Professional-level task. For root module variables the order, highest first, is: `-var` and `-var-file` on the command line (in the order given) together with variables set in HCP Terraform; `*.auto.tfvars` and `*.auto.tfvars.json` in lexical order; `terraform.tfvars.json`; `terraform.tfvars`; `TF_VAR_` environment variables; and the `default`. Conflicts are not errors; only assigning one variable twice in the same file is. Worked case: default `tiny`, `TF_VAR_size=xlarge`, `terraform.tfvars` small, `prod.auto.tfvars` large and `-var-file=ci.tfvars` medium gives medium. Lexical order is character order: `10-base.auto.tfvars` sorts before `2-team.auto.tfvars`, so the team file wins, and layered prefixes should be zero-padded. In HCP Terraform, workspace variables and variable sets rank above auto files and `terraform.tfvars`, so a workspace value of 5 beats `instance_count = 2` committed in `prod.auto.tfvars`. A value kept in two places means the reviewed file may not be what the run uses, so keep each variable in one place.

concepts.heading: Version Constraints Across Modules and the Lock File
concepts.body: A single provider version is installed for the whole configuration, and Terraform must satisfy the constraints of the root module and every child module together. If the root says `>= 5.0, < 5.10` and a registry module says `>= 5.20`, the intersection is empty and `terraform init` reports that no available release matches, listing which modules asked for what. Fix by raising the root bound after testing, choosing an older module version with a lower minimum, or relaxing one side. The recommendation for a shared module is a minimum only, `>=` the first release with the features it uses, because tighter pins in widely used modules block consumers; the root decides the final range. A pre-release such as `2.1.0-beta` is matched only by an exact version (`=` or no operator), never by `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=` or `~>`. The lock file `.terraform.lock.hcl` records providers only. Remote modules are not remembered: a fresh CI workspace with `version = "~> 5.0"` takes the newest release in range, while a laptop that installed earlier keeps its copy, which explains plans that differ. Pin third-party modules to an exact version and move the pin in a reviewed change.

concepts.heading: Upgrading Deliberately and Changing Provider Source
concepts.body: `terraform init` reuses lock file selections and leaves installed modules alone, only installing what is new. `terraform init -upgrade` ignores lock selections, picks the newest provider matching the constraints, rewrites the lock file, and also updates installed child modules to the latest source matching their version constraints or refs. It never edits `.tf` files, changes the CLI version or migrates state. Review the lock file diff and the plan afterwards, in a lower environment first. To make CI fail when init would change the committed lock file, use `terraform init -lockfile=readonly`: it suppresses lock changes but still verifies installed packages against the recorded checksums, and it conflicts with `-upgrade`. Do not confuse it with `-backend=false` or `-get=false`. Each resource in state records its provider's fully qualified source address, so when a team moves from `hashicorp/aws` to an in-house `registry.acme.corp/acme/aws` and edits `required_providers`, plan fails because existing entries name the old address. Run `terraform state replace-provider registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws registry.acme.corp/acme/aws`, which writes a state backup first and asks for confirmation, then re-run init.

examPoints: A question where a script fails on terraform output -raw is testing that -raw handles only string, number and boolean, so lists and maps need -json with jq.
A question about reading another HCP Terraform workspace without full state access is testing tfe_outputs, which is not subject to remote state sharing but needs a token with permission.
A question where CI differs from a laptop after a new release is testing that the lock file covers providers only, so remote modules need an exact version pin.

quiz.q: A directory holds `10-base.auto.tfvars` (tier = "base") and `2-team.auto.tfvars` (tier = "team"). Nothing else sets tier. Which value does the root module use?
choices: base, because the file with the larger number loads first and the first value wins
team, because files load in lexical order and the later file wins
An error, because the same variable is set in two files
base, because numeric prefixes are compared as numbers
quiz.explain: Lexical order compares character by character, so 10-base sorts before 2-team and the later file wins. Choice C is wrong because duplicates are an error only inside one file; D is wrong because prefixes are not compared numerically.

quiz.q: The root module requires aws `>= 5.0, < 5.10` and a registry module requires `>= 5.20`. terraform init finds no available release. What is the cause?
choices: Terraform needs one version satisfying the root and all child module constraints together, and the ranges do not overlap
The lock file lists a different platform, so init cannot download the provider
Pre-release versions are blocked by the >= operator in the child module
Child modules may use their own provider version, and the registry rejected the second one
quiz.explain: All constraints are intersected because one provider version serves the whole configuration. Choice B concerns hashes, not ranges; C is unrelated to these numbers; D is wrong since a single version is shared.

days.recap: Output: -raw scalars only, -json for lists; tfe_outputs avoids full state access. Precedence: -var/-var-file and HCP vars > auto.tfvars (lexical) > terraform.tfvars > TF_VAR > default. Constraints intersect; modules want >= only; lock file is providers only; init -upgrade, -lockfile=readonly, state replace-provider.

days.title: CI/CD Pipeline Stages and Deployment Strategies with Terraform

concepts.heading: Pipeline Stages and Credential-Free Gates
concepts.body: A good pipeline is a sequence of gates, cheapest first, so most mistakes fail in seconds and without cloud access. Two gates need no credentials. `terraform fmt -check` reads only local files and exits 0 when formatting is canonical and non-zero, with file names, otherwise. By default `fmt` scans only the current directory, so a pipeline that must catch a badly formatted module under `modules/network/` uses `terraform fmt -check -recursive`. `terraform init -backend=false` followed by `terraform validate` catches syntax, attribute-name and type errors without touching the backend or any API. Validate does not test remote services, so an instance size that has the right type but that no provider API accepts passes validation and fails at plan; move such checks earlier with variable `validation` blocks or preconditions. Anything that reads real objects, a normal plan, a refresh-only plan and apply, needs the backend and provider credentials, so it belongs in a later stage on a runner that has them.

concepts.heading: Approval Gates and Saved Plan Artifacts
concepts.body: An approval gate is meaningful only if the thing reviewed is the thing that runs. If a pipeline plans on merge, a reviewer approves, and a later job runs `terraform apply -auto-approve` without a plan file, apply creates a new plan; anything that changed in between (another merge, a console edit, another pipeline) can appear unapproved, which is how a database got deleted that the reviewed plan never mentioned. The fix is to save the plan with `-out`, show it for review (`terraform show`), place the manual approval after it and apply that same file; if state moved meanwhile, Terraform refuses the stale plan. When plan and apply are separate jobs on different runners, remember: the artifact holds the full configuration and variable values and stores sensitive values in cleartext, so restrict access; the apply job must run `terraform init` with the same lock file and Terraform version because the plan file does not carry providers; and `-input=false` with no plan file and no `-auto-approve` fails, because with prompts disabled Terraform assumes you do not approve. Apply a saved plan or use `-auto-approve` deliberately, for example on an ephemeral environment.

concepts.heading: Exit Codes and HCP Terraform Runs
concepts.body: `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` returns 0 for success with no changes, 1 for an error and 2 for success with changes. A pipeline can then branch: 0 skips approval and apply, 2 raises the approval gate, 1 fails the build. A step that treats every non-zero code as failure will break on valid plans with pending changes, so capture the status and treat 2 explicitly. In HCP Terraform, a workspace connected to a repository starts a speculative plan when a pull request opens; it shows possible changes, is checked against policies, can never be applied and reruns when the pull request is updated. Pull requests from forks do not get one, to avoid running untrusted code or exposing sensitive information (on Terraform Enterprise an administrator can allow it), which explains a fork contribution with no plan while internal branches get one. Runs created through the API with the save-plan option are never auto-applied, even in a workspace with auto-apply enabled; they wait for confirmation, are discarded automatically if another run applies first, and ignore the per-workspace queue while planning. They suit custom CI that wants explicit approval of an exact plan.

concepts.heading: Blue/Green and Canary as Modeling Choices
concepts.body: Terraform has no deployment engine: it applies the state you declare, so a strategy is a way of modeling it. Blue/green keeps two complete stacks defined and uses one routing object, such as a load balancer listener, DNS weight or routing rule, to decide which receives traffic. A single variable such as `active_color` that changes only the listener's target makes cutover a tiny, reviewable plan, and rollback is the same one-line change because the old stack is still running. Remove the old stack later in a separate apply. A canary release (5 percent, 25, 100) needs configuration that feeds a weight variable (`canary_weight`) into a weighted target group or record, plus orchestration Terraform does not provide: the pipeline applies one step, evaluates metrics from a monitoring system, and runs the next apply only if the gate passes, or reapplies the previous value. Timers and provisioner sleeps are fragile and do not look at health. Each step should be a small plan; avoid `-target` for routine releases, because the docs reserve it for exceptional situations.

concepts.heading: Rolling Changes and Progressive Environments
concepts.body: A plan expresses the final state. If an AMI change forces replacement of twelve instances in one resource, the plan contains twelve replacements and the apply walks them as the graph allows; Terraform has no batch size. Plain Terraform can still roll in batches: put the instances in a `for_each` map keyed by group (`batch1`..`batch3`) with a per-group version value and move one group per apply, verifying between applies. Alternatively delegate rolling to a platform feature such as an autoscaling group's instance refresh and let Terraform change only the launch template. For promotion from dev to staging to prod, promote the same commit or module version tag through each environment and let environments differ only in variable values, each with its own backend and credentials. Per-environment branches or copied directories drift apart, and a floating branch reference makes what is deployed depend on the moment of the last init. In HCP Terraform, a run trigger queues a run in a workspace when a source workspace applies successfully, but runs created by a trigger do not auto-apply unless Auto-apply run triggers is enabled, which makes a handy promotion gate. Preview environments get their own state and are destroyed with it when the pull request closes.

examPoints: A question about an unformatted module that reached main is testing that terraform fmt -check covers only the current directory unless -recursive is added.
A question where the reviewed plan differs from what applied is testing that an approval gate must cover a saved plan file applied afterward, not a second fresh plan.
A question about canary or blue/green with Terraform is testing that cutover is a small variable-driven diff and that health checks and pacing come from pipeline orchestration, not from Terraform.

quiz.q: A pipeline step runs `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` and the build is marked failed on every run that has valid pending changes. What explains this?
choices: The flag makes plan return 1 whenever changes exist
Exit code 2 means success with changes, and the step treats any non-zero status as an error
The flag turns plan into an interactive prompt that times out
Exit code 0 is returned for changes, so the pipeline sees a missing apply
quiz.explain: With the flag: 0 no changes, 1 error, 2 changes present. The step must handle 2 explicitly. Choice A confuses the error code, C invents a prompt, and D reverses the meaning of 0.

quiz.q: A team promotes a change through dev, staging and prod and wants staging results to predict prod. Which practice fits best?
choices: Keep a branch per environment and cherry-pick fixes after each test
Point every environment at the main branch tip so they stay current
Copy the directory for each environment and edit the sizes by hand
Promote the same commit or module version tag, differing only in per-environment variable values
quiz.explain: Promotion works when the promoted unit is fixed and only inputs differ. Choices A and C drift apart, and B makes the deployed code depend on the moment of the last init.

days.recap: Cheap gates first: fmt -check -recursive, init -backend=false + validate (no API checks). Apply the exact saved plan after approval. -detailed-exitcode: 2 means changes. No speculative plans for forks; saved-plan runs never auto-apply. Blue/green = routing variable; canary needs pipeline metrics gates.

days.title: Dynamic Provider Credentials and Variable Files in Pipelines

concepts.heading: How Dynamic Credentials Work
concepts.body: Dynamic provider credentials replace long-lived cloud keys with a trust relationship. You configure the cloud platform to trust HCP Terraform as an OpenID Connect issuer and define rules for which workspaces and runs may assume which role. Then, for each plan and apply, HCP Terraform generates a workload identity token (OIDC) with claims about the organization, project, workspace and run stage, and sends it to the platform. The platform verifies the token with HCP Terraform's public signing key and, if its rules pass, returns fresh temporary credentials that HCP Terraform places in the run environment for the provider. Nothing static is stored in the workspace, so there is nothing to rotate or leak. On AWS the switch is the environment variable `TFC_AWS_PROVIDER_AUTH=true` together with a role ARN variable. The provider block must not fight this: the docs say to avoid the other arguments or methods in the provider's authentication documentation (such as static `access_key` and `secret_key` arguments or competing AWS environment variables) because they may interfere with dynamic credentials, which is why a workspace can still run as an old IAM user after dynamic credentials were enabled. Pass a region (the `region` argument or `AWS_REGION`).

concepts.heading: Writing the Trust Policy
concepts.body: The identity provider in AWS only trusts tokens from HCP Terraform's issuer; the role trust policy decides which tokens may assume the role. Tokens carry `aud`, the audience, which defaults to `aws.workload.identity` (or the value of `TFC_AWS_WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_AUDIENCE`), and `sub`, shaped like `organization:ORG:project:PROJECT:workspace:WORKSPACE:run_phase:PHASE`. The default audience is public knowledge, so a condition on `aud` alone lets any workspace in any HCP Terraform organization that presents such a token assume the role. The docs say to check at minimum the audience and the organization name, and better the project and workspace through `sub`. Use `StringEquals` for one exact subject, or `StringLike` with `*` to cover a family of workspaces, scoped to the organization and project but no wider. Because `sub` ends in `run_phase:plan` or `run_phase:apply`, the run phase can be matched too. If plan and apply need different permissions, create two roles with two trust policies. If both phases can share one role, a single trust policy using `StringLike` with `*` after `run_phase:` accepts either.

concepts.heading: Per-Phase Roles, Sharing and Other Clouds
concepts.body: To make plans read-only and applies writable on AWS, create two roles whose trust policies match `run_phase:plan` and `run_phase:apply`, and set `TFC_AWS_PLAN_ROLE_ARN` and `TFC_AWS_APPLY_ROLE_ARN`. `TFC_AWS_RUN_ROLE_ARN` is the fallback when a phase-specific variable is not set. To share one role across forty workspaces in a project, put `TFC_AWS_PROVIDER_AUTH=true` and `TFC_AWS_RUN_ROLE_ARN` in a variable set applied to the project, and write a `sub` condition with `StringLike` wide enough for those workspaces; one change in the set then updates all of them. Azure uses federated identity credentials whose subject identifier must match the token subject exactly, as a direct string comparison, so each workspace needs two federated credentials, one for `run_phase:plan` and one for `run_phase:apply`; the audience defaults to `api://AzureADTokenExchange`. A symptom of the mistake is plans that authenticate while every apply fails. A workspace can also hold several configurations of one provider type by appending a tag to variable names (`[VAR_NAME]_[TAG]`); HCP Terraform then supplies a variable such as `tfc_aws_dynamic_credentials` with a default object and an aliases map, and each provider block, the default one included, must be mapped from it.

concepts.heading: Vault-Backed Credentials and Terraform Enterprise
concepts.body: Native dynamic credentials require the cloud platform to verify tokens itself. On Terraform Enterprise that means the cloud must reach the instance's OIDC metadata endpoints, `/.well-known/openid-configuration` and `/.well-known/jwks`. A company that will not expose those endpoints to the public internet can use Vault-backed dynamic credentials instead, which the HCP Terraform documentation describes: Vault trusts the workload identity token, and its AWS, GCP or Azure secrets engine generates the short-lived cloud credentials. Only Vault needs to reach the metadata endpoints, which do not have to be public, and the docs mention an air-gapped setup is possible when Vault is in the same secure network. Both approaches give each run short-lived credentials with no static secret in the workspace; the difference is who verifies the token and where the trust rules live. Vault-backed is the documented answer when network exposure of the Terraform instance is the constraint. In either case the permissions come from the role the token is allowed to assume, so least privilege is set in the cloud role and its trust policy.

concepts.heading: tfvars Files and Precedence in Pipelines
concepts.body: Without flags, Terraform loads only `terraform.tfvars`, `terraform.tfvars.json` and files ending in `.auto.tfvars` or `.auto.tfvars.json`. A file named `prod.tfvars` is ignored unless passed with `-var-file`, so per-environment files are either given the `.auto.tfvars` suffix (always on) or kept plain and selected explicitly in each pipeline step. Order of precedence, highest first: `-var` and `-var-file` on the command line and variables from HCP Terraform; `*.auto.tfvars` in lexical order; `terraform.tfvars.json`; `terraform.tfvars`; `TF_VAR_` environment variables; the `default`. With `terraform.tfvars` small, `prod.auto.tfvars` large and `TF_VAR_size=medium`, a plain `terraform plan` uses large. Numeric prefixes layer a base file under an override (`10-base`, `20-prod`) but are compared as text, so zero-pad them. Inside HCP Terraform, workspace variables and variable sets beat an auto.tfvars file in the uploaded directory. Variable sets have two layers: a priority variable set overrides variables with the same key at more specific scopes, with a prioritized global set at the top, while non-priority sets rank below workspace-specific variables, so a workspace variable overwrites them. Use priority sets for values that must not be overridden locally, such as a mandatory region.

examPoints: A question about a role trust policy checking only aud is testing that the default audience is public, so sub (organization, project, workspace, run phase) must be matched.
A question where plans authenticate but applies fail on Azure is testing that federated credential subjects match as exact strings, so both run_phase:plan and run_phase:apply credentials are needed.

A question about which tfvars file wins is testing the order: command line and HCP Terraform variables, auto.tfvars in lexical order, terraform.tfvars, TF_VAR, default, with priority variable sets above everything.

quiz.q: Dynamic AWS credentials are enabled in a workspace, yet runs still act as an old IAM user. The AWS provider block sets access_key and secret_key from variables. What should the team do?
choices: Raise the token lifetime so the temporary credentials outlast the static ones
Remove static credential arguments and conflicting AWS environment variables from the configuration
Add a second trust policy statement that allows the old IAM user to assume the role
Move the static keys into a non-priority variable set so they rank lower
quiz.explain: The docs say other authentication arguments and methods can interfere with dynamic credentials, so static keys and competing environment variables must go. Choice A and C do not change which credentials the provider uses, and D only changes variable precedence, not how the provider authenticates.

quiz.q: An organization-wide variable set marked as a priority set defines region = us-east-1 and applies to all workspaces. One workspace has its own variable region = eu-west-1. Which value do its runs use?
choices: eu-west-1, because workspace variables always override variable sets
The one declared in the repository's prod.auto.tfvars, because files in version control are authoritative
An error, because the same key is defined twice
us-east-1, because a priority global variable set overrides all other variables with the same key
quiz.explain: A prioritized global variable set sits at the top of the order. Only non-priority sets rank below workspace variables (choice A), auto files rank lower still (B), and conflicts are not errors (C).

days.recap: Dynamic credentials: OIDC token per plan/apply, trust policy must match sub, not just public aud. Separate plan/apply roles; Azure needs one federated credential per phase. Remove static keys. Vault-backed avoids exposing Enterprise endpoints. tfvars: only auto files load; priority variable sets win.

days.title: Secrets in Terraform: State and Plan Exposure, Ephemeral Values, Write-Only Arguments and Rotation

concepts.heading: sensitive Hides Display, Not Storage
concepts.body: Marking a variable or output `sensitive = true` changes how Terraform displays a value: it is redacted in CLI output and in the HCP Terraform UI, and any expression that references it is treated as sensitive too. It does not change what Terraform stores. State and plan files still contain the real value, so anyone who can read them can read the secret, and `terraform output -raw` or `-json` prints a sensitive output in plain text. A typical failing review: a module passes `var.db_password` (sensitive) to `aws_db_instance`, the plan shows `(sensitive value)`, yet an auditor opens the state file and sees the password. The fix is not another flag on the variable but keeping the value out of state altogether, plus protecting the state backend as the secret store it effectively is. The same holds for saved plans: `terraform plan -out` writes the full configuration, all values for planned changes and the input variables, and the documentation says sensitive data is saved in cleartext in the plan file. A pipeline that uploads `tfplan` as a build artifact must therefore restrict who can download it and keep retention short, exactly as for state.

concepts.heading: Ephemeral Resources and Write-Only Arguments
concepts.body: Only ephemeral values are omitted from state and plan files: variables and child module outputs with `ephemeral = true`, `ephemeral` blocks and write-only arguments. An ephemeral resource such as `ephemeral "random_password" "db" {}` exists only during the current operation and is never written to state or plan. A write-only argument, usually named with a `_wo` suffix such as `password_wo`, is a managed-resource argument that the provider uses when it creates or updates the object and that Terraform then discards. It needs Terraform 1.11 or later and provider support. To get a generated password into a database without a trace in state, feed the ephemeral value into the write-only argument: `password_wo = ephemeral.random_password.db.result`. Replacing `password = random_password.db.result` with a sensitive variable would still store it. Write-only arguments accept ephemeral and non-ephemeral values, but a literal string would still sit in the configuration, so HashiCorp recommends feeding them from an ephemeral resource. Because the value is not stored, the plan cannot show a diff for it, which matters for rotation.

concepts.heading: Where an Ephemeral Value May Be Used
concepts.body: Terraform allows references to ephemeral values only where the value cannot be persisted: `locals`, `variable` blocks with `ephemeral`, child module `output` blocks with `ephemeral`, write-only arguments of managed resources, other `ephemeral` blocks, `provider` blocks, and provisioner and connection blocks. Anywhere else, for example an ordinary resource argument, a data source or a root output, planning returns an error. That list answers the question of a team that reads a secret with `ephemeral "aws_ssm_parameter" "api"` and wants to use `.value`: a write-only argument and a provider configuration are valid, an ordinary argument or a root output is not. Ephemeral outputs are the way a module hands a short-lived credential to its caller during one run, but the `ephemeral` argument on an output is allowed only in child modules, since a root output is persisted so that `terraform output` and other configurations can read it. If a root module re-exports `module.auth.token` as an ephemeral output, Terraform rejects the configuration; the root should consume the value in an ephemeral context such as a provider block instead. Note that `sensitive` on a child output is a different control: it hides the value on screen but the value still reaches state.

concepts.heading: Rotation: Version Arguments and Vault Leases
concepts.body: A rotation can be invisible. Terraform sends a write-only argument to the provider on every operation, but it keeps no prior value, so a new value alone produces no plan diff. A team sets `password_wo = var.new_password` and `password_wo_version = 1`, the pipeline supplies the rotated secret, and the plan says no changes while the database keeps the old password. The provider's version argument is the stored signal: Terraform does store that number, so incrementing it in the same change as the new value produces an update and the provider applies the new write-only value. Good practice ties the version to the secrets manager's own version metadata so that rotation in the store drives the update. Dynamic secrets have a lifecycle too. An `ephemeral` block opens when Terraform needs it (for a Vault secret the provider obtains a lease), renews if the operation outlasts the expiration, and closes after dependent providers finish in that phase, which for Vault explicitly ends the lease so the credentials are revoked immediately. If an input to an ephemeral resource is unknown until apply, such as the ID of a secret version created in the same run, Terraform defers the ephemeral resource to the apply stage; a data source for the same read would have stored the value in state.

concepts.heading: Leak Paths Outside State: VCS, Variables and Credentials
concepts.body: Variable files are plain text and Git keeps history. A reviewer who finds `prod.auto.tfvars` with `db_password` committed two weeks ago must treat the secret as compromised: deleting the file does not remove it from earlier commits, clones or forks. The complete fix has three parts: rotate the credential, remove and ignore the file (rewriting history is an extra clean-up, never a substitute for rotation) and re-supply the value from outside the repository, such as an HCP Terraform sensitive variable, an environment variable or an ephemeral read from a secrets manager. A related review point concerns provider credentials stored in a workspace. A sensitive Terraform variable is unreadable in the UI and API, but Terraform runs receive the full text of all variable values and may print them in logs or state if the configuration sends them to an output or a resource argument. A provider credential supplied as an environment variable is read by the provider process and is not referenced from the configuration, so that path does not exist; both categories can be marked sensitive. Better still is to remove the stored secret: dynamic credentials, either through the platform's workload identity or through Vault, issue short-lived values per run (covered on the next day).

examPoints: A question where a sensitive variable still appears in the state file is testing that sensitive only redacts display; the answer that keeps it out of state uses an ephemeral value with a write-only argument.
A question about a rotation that produces an empty plan is testing the write-only version argument: increment it together with the new secret so that the stored number changes.

A question about an ephemeral value used in an ordinary resource argument, a data source or a root output is testing the list of allowed ephemeral contexts; locals, write-only arguments, provider blocks and child module ephemeral outputs are valid.

quiz.q: A config passes `random_password.db.result` to the `password` argument of `aws_db_instance`. Security wants the generated password in neither resource's state entry. Which change achieves this?
choices: Mark the `random_password` result as sensitive in an output and keep `password` as the argument
Store the password in a variable with `sensitive = true` and pass `var.password` to `password`
Make the generator an `ephemeral "random_password"` block and pass its result to a write-only argument such as `password_wo`
Keep the resources and add the `-out` plan file to a private artifact store
quiz.explain: The ephemeral block is never written to state or plan, and the write-only argument is discarded after the provider uses it, so neither entry holds the password. Choices A and B only hide the display and the value stays in state; choice D protects a plan file but does nothing for state.

quiz.q: A database sets `password_wo = var.new_password` and `password_wo_version = 1`. The secret was rotated and the pipeline passes the new value, but `terraform plan` shows no changes. What is the correct explanation and fix?
choices: Terraform keeps no prior value of a write-only argument, so there is nothing to compare; increment the version argument with the new value
Write-only arguments are refreshed only by `terraform apply -refresh-only`, so run that first
The variable must be marked `sensitive = true` for Terraform to detect the new value
State locking hides the diff; force-unlock the workspace and plan again
quiz.explain: The write-only value is never stored, so only the stored version number can signal a change. Choice B is wrong because refresh does not read an argument that was never saved, and choices C and D concern display and locking, not change detection.

days.recap: Sensitive hides display only; state and saved plans hold cleartext. Ephemeral resources, variables and child outputs plus write-only arguments keep secrets out of state, usable only in allowed contexts. Rotate with the *_wo_version argument, let Vault leases close with the run, and never leave secrets in VCS.

days.title: Pipeline Identity, Policy Sets and Risky Changes: Least Privilege, Sentinel/OPA Scope and Plan Gates

concepts.heading: Workload Identity and Trust Policies
concepts.body: With dynamic provider credentials, HCP Terraform generates a workload identity token (a JWT) for each plan or apply, signed with its private key and expiring at the end of the plan or apply timeout. The cloud verifies it with the platform's public key and returns temporary credentials for the role named in the workspace variables, so nothing long-lived is stored. That is the direct answer to a team that rotates an IAM user key by hand in a sensitive environment variable. The trust policy is where least privilege is decided. The `sub` claim reads `organization:ORG:project:PROJECT:workspace:WS:run_phase:PHASE`, and HashiCorp warns to check at minimum `aud` (the intended audience, so a token issued for one system cannot be replayed against another) and the organization name, which the `sub` claim carries together with project, workspace and run phase. A `StringLike` pattern with `*` for project and workspace lets every workspace in the organization, including a sandbox any developer can run, assume a production admin role; if the organization name is not matched at all, any workspace on HCP Terraform could reach the cloud resources. Use the exact project and workspace, and wildcard only the run phase when plan and apply need the same access. Claims such as `terraform_run_id` change on every run, so they are useless for trust matching.

concepts.heading: Separate Plan and Apply Roles, and Vault-Backed Credentials
concepts.body: The `sub` claim ends in `run_phase:plan` or `run_phase:apply`, so trust policies can tell the phases apart. For a workspace whose plans should only read and whose applies must write, create two roles, each trusting one phase, and set the environment variables `TFC_AWS_PLAN_ROLE_ARN` and `TFC_AWS_APPLY_ROLE_ARN`; if the plan variable is absent, `TFC_AWS_RUN_ROLE_ARN` is used for both. A wildcard on `run_phase` or a longer session duration cannot create this separation. There are two forms of dynamic credentials. The first relies on the cloud trusting the platform's OIDC identity and verifying tokens through its public metadata endpoints. The second, Vault-backed dynamic credentials, authenticates the run's token to Vault, whose secrets engines (AWS, GCP, Azure) generate short-lived credentials. The documentation positions Vault-backed credentials for teams that want a central place to manage cloud credentials and want to avoid exposing the platform's OIDC metadata endpoints publicly. A self-hosted Terraform Enterprise instance with no public metadata endpoint that still needs short-lived AWS credentials therefore fits the Vault-backed form.

concepts.heading: Permissions Add Up and Connected Systems Count
concepts.body: HCP Terraform permissions are additive across organization, project and workspace scopes: a team's effective permission is the highest level it holds from any scope. If a team has the Read role on workspace prod-net but also holds the organization permission Manage all workspaces, its members can queue and confirm applies there. The reverse does not apply: a lower organization permission such as View all workspaces never overrides a higher workspace role. Least-privilege reviews must therefore audit all scopes together and grant only the workspace or project roles that are intended. Permissions of integrated systems count too. In a VCS-connected workspace, anyone who can merge to the linked branch can queue plans, even without permission to queue plans and even if they are not an organization member; with auto-apply on, a merge starts a run that applies without a confirmation step. Developers with only Read on the workspace but merge rights on main therefore hold an effective write path. Treat merge rights as workspace write rights: protect the branch, require reviews, limit who can merge and turn auto-apply off on sensitive workspaces so a human or policy gate confirms the plan.

concepts.heading: Policy Sets: Scope, Enforcement and Who May Override
concepts.body: A policy set is a collection of policies, and scope lives on the set, not on the individual policy. It can be global, or limited to projects, workspaces or workspaces with specific tags, and it can exclude a project, workspace or tag. A tagging rule for every workspace except those in Sandbox, now and for workspaces created later, is a global policy set with Sandbox excluded; manual attachment has gaps whenever someone forgets. A baseline can run globally while stricter sets cover selected projects. Each policy has a framework, Sentinel or OPA, fixed at creation, and a set contains policies of one framework only. Sentinel levels are advisory (reported, never stops), soft mandatory (stops the run in the Policy Override state, and a user allowed to override can continue) and hard mandatory (stops until the configuration is fixed); if the set enables the override option, permitted users can override even hard failures. Team permissions decide who: no policy overrides, delegate policy overrides, or manage policy overrides. The Manage policies permission lets security staff write policies and set enforcement and implies reading runs on all workspaces, but not changing infrastructure. An OPA policy is registered with a query such as `data.terraform.policies.public_ingress.deny` whose result must be an array; an empty array passes, and the plan is available as `input.plan`.

concepts.heading: Spotting and Blocking Risky Changes
concepts.body: Three layers catch dangerous changes. First, read the plan as data: `terraform show -json tfplan` has a `resource_changes` array, each entry with `change.actions`. A replacement appears as `["delete","create"]` or, with `create_before_destroy`, `["create","delete"]`, so a gate must test that the list contains both actions; matching only `["delete"]` misses replacements. The optional `action_reason` explains why: `delete_because_no_resource_config` and `delete_because_no_module` mark deletions caused by removed configuration, for example a deleted `module "db"` call, while `replace_because_cannot_update` and `replace_because_tainted` mark routine replacements. Second, `prevent_destroy = true` makes Terraform reject any plan that destroys the object, including a forced replacement, so changing a non-updatable argument of a protected database errors and the safe path is a planned migration; it does not stop destruction when the resource block itself is removed, because lifecycle rules are not recorded in state. Third, a mandatory Sentinel or OPA policy over `resource_changes` also covers block removal. A `check` block, by contrast, only warns after the plan or apply and, with workspace health checks, is re-evaluated on a schedule; it never blocks.

examPoints: A question about long-lived keys in a workspace is testing dynamic provider credentials: a token per run, trusted by `aud` and `sub`, with separate plan and apply roles when permissions differ.

A question about a team whose Read role still allows applies is testing additive permissions across scopes, and merge rights on a VCS-driven workspace with auto-apply are an equivalent hidden write path.

A question about preventing or detecting destruction expects a layered answer: prevent_destroy for plans, a mandatory policy on resource_changes for block removal, and check blocks only as non-blocking warnings.

quiz.q: An AWS role trusts HCP Terraform with `StringLike` on `sub` of `organization:acme:project:*:workspace:*:run_phase:*` and grants admin access to production. What is the risk, and what narrows it?
choices: Every workspace in the organization, including a sandbox one, can assume the production role; match the exact project and workspace, wildcarding only the run phase
Only workspaces in the acme organization with apply permission can assume the role, so the pattern is safe as written
Tokens never expire under this pattern; shorten the session duration on the role
The `aud` claim already limits the role to one workspace, so no change is needed
quiz.explain: The wildcards let any acme workspace assume the role. Choice B is wrong because the cloud sees only the token claims, not HCP Terraform permissions, and D is wrong because `aud` identifies the audience and not the workspace.

quiz.q: A developer deletes a `module "db"` call from the root. A review gate must flag deletions caused by removed configuration but let routine replacements pass. Which gate design is correct?
choices: Block any plan whose actions contain only `["delete"]` and ignore all replacements
Require extra approval when actions contain delete and the reason is `delete_because_no_resource_config` or `delete_because_no_module`, letting `replace_because_cannot_update` pass
Rely on `prevent_destroy`, which also stops deletion when a module call is removed
Use a `check` block, which stops the run when a resource is deleted
quiz.explain: The two removal reasons identify deletions caused by removed configuration while replacement reasons are routine. Choice C is wrong because prevent_destroy is not recorded in state and does not protect removed blocks, and choice D is wrong because a failed check only warns.

days.recap: Replace stored keys with dynamic credentials and trust only the exact organization, project, workspace, aud and sub, with separate plan and apply roles. Permissions are additive and merge rights count. Policy sets scope by global, project, workspace or tag; gate risky changes on resource_changes actions and reasons.

days.title: Module Design: When to Extract, Composition, moved Blocks, Providers and the Output Contract

concepts.heading: When a Module Pays Off
concepts.body: A module is a set of resources managed together behind an interface of input variables and outputs. Its child resources become part of the caller's plan, apply and state, so a module is a unit of reuse and standardization and not a unit of isolation: a failed apply inside one module affects the whole run. Splitting a directory into `network.tf` and `database.tf` organizes code without any module. Sound reasons to extract are a pattern used repeatedly with small parameter differences, or a set of resources that encode decisions such as defaults, naming, composition of several resources and validation. A pass-through wrapper is the counter-example: a module `s3_bucket` with 25 variables passed one-to-one to a single `aws_s3_bucket`, no defaults and no extra logic, encodes nothing. Callers must learn both the module and the resource, and the author must update the wrapper whenever the provider adds, renames or deprecates an argument. It would be justified by default encryption, versioning, public access blocks and tags, or by creating the bucket, policy and lifecycle rules together. Ask what decision the module makes for the caller before extracting.

concepts.heading: Composition and Keeping the Tree Flat
concepts.body: Terraform's composition guidance favors dependency inversion: a module declares what it needs as inputs and the caller decides where those objects come from. An `app` module that must use a managed VPC in production and an existing shared VPC in development should take `vpc_id` and `subnet_ids` as inputs; the caller passes `data.aws_vpc.shared.id` in development and `module.network.subnet_ids` in production. The alternative, a module that creates its own network behind conditionals, grows complex and cannot coexist with a network owned elsewhere. The same design keeps working when the network later moves into its own configuration. The guidance also recommends a flat tree, about one level of child modules connected by expressions in the root. In a chain `platform` calls `network` calls `subnets` calls `routing`, a team that needs a custom routing policy finds that every level must forward a variable. Instead, the root calls `network` and `routing` as siblings and passes `module.network.subnet_ids` into `routing`; a caller with a special need can swap one building block for its own, and the wiring is visible in one place.

concepts.heading: Refactoring Safely with moved Blocks
concepts.body: Terraform tracks objects by address, and `aws_instance.web` and `module.web.aws_instance.web` are different addresses. Moving a resource into a new module without telling Terraform plans a destroy of the old address and a create of the new one. A `moved` block (`from = aws_instance.web`, `to = module.web.aws_instance.web`) lets Terraform rename the state entry before planning, so the plan shows no destroy. The same mechanism covers other refactors. Switching `count` to `for_each` needs one block per instance, such as `from = aws_subnet.private[0]` to `aws_subnet.private["a"]`; put inside a shared module, every caller that upgrades picks up the mapping on its next plan, and new callers ignore it. Adding `count = 3` to a module call with `moved { from = module.a  to = module.a[2] }` treats the existing objects as instance 2, so the plan creates only `module.a[0]` and `module.a[1]`. When a grown module is split into `x` and `y`, keep the old module as a backward-compatible shim that calls both and carries `moved` blocks; references in them resolve relative to the containing module, and a module may only make moved statements about its own objects and its children, not a sibling's.

concepts.heading: Providers and Modules
concepts.body: Provider configurations are global to a configuration and may be defined only in the root module. A reusable module must not contain `provider` blocks: a module with its own provider block cannot be called with `count`, `for_each` or `depends_on` and fails with an error such as `Module does not support count`, and removing the module would also remove the configuration its resources need for destruction. The module declares what it needs in `required_providers` (including aliases through `configuration_aliases`), and the caller passes configurations with `providers`. Configurations are inherited, requirements are not: a child module that creates `datadog_monitor` resources without its own `required_providers` entry for `DataDog/datadog` does not inherit the root's source address, and Terraform may look for a `hashicorp/datadog` provider instead. Provider association is static because Terraform decides it before expanding `count` and `for_each`. A single module call with `for_each` over three regions cannot select `aws.eu`, `aws.us` and `aws.ap` per instance; write one `module` block per configuration, for example `providers = { aws = aws.eu }` in each. Every instance of one module call receives the same provider configurations.

concepts.heading: The Output Contract and Versioning
concepts.body: Inputs and outputs are the module's public interface, and anything exposed can be depended on. An output of `value = aws_db_instance.this` puts the entire provider schema into the contract: a provider rename or a change of resource type breaks callers although the module's code did not change, and it carries attributes nobody asked for. Expose stable names with descriptions, such as `endpoint`, `arn` and `port`, and mark secrets `sensitive = true`. Registry modules use semantic versions and callers write constraints like `~> 2.0` on that basis. Renaming or removing an input or output is breaking and belongs in a major release; adding an optional input or a new output is a minor release. A maintainer who renames `vpc_id` to `network_id` in 2.3.0 breaks every `~> 2.0` caller; the graceful path adds `network_id`, keeps `vpc_id` (noting it as deprecated) and removes it in 3.0.0. Instance keys are part of the contract as well: changing a resource from `count` to `for_each` without `moved` blocks forces replacement. Ephemeral outputs may be declared only in child modules, never in the root, and their value must come from an ephemeral context.

examPoints: A question that offers a module with identical arguments to one resource is testing abstraction: extract when the module encodes defaults, composition or validation, not for pass-through wrappers.
A question about a refactor that plans a destroy and create is testing moved blocks for new addresses, including instance keys, with the mapping placed in the module so callers inherit it.
A question about a module failing with count or for_each is testing that provider blocks belong only in the root, and per-instance provider selection needs separate module blocks.

quiz.q: A team moves `aws_instance.web` from the root module into `module "web"` containing the same resource. The plan shows `aws_instance.web` to be destroyed and `module.web.aws_instance.web` to be created. Which change gives a plan with no destroy?
choices: Add `lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }` to the resource inside the module
Run `terraform apply -refresh-only` before planning
Set `prevent_destroy = true` on the resource in the root
Add `moved { from = aws_instance.web  to = module.web.aws_instance.web }` to the configuration
quiz.explain: The moved block maps the old state address to the new one before planning. Choice A only reorders a replacement, choice B updates attributes and not addresses, and choice C would make the plan error instead of fixing it.

quiz.q: A shared module adds `provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1" }`, and a caller that sets `count = 2` on the module call now fails with `Module does not support count`. What is the correct fix?
choices: Remove the provider block from the module, declare the provider in its `required_providers`, and configure it in the root, passing it with `providers` if needed
Add `depends_on` to the module call so the provider initializes first
Replace `count` with `for_each` on the module call, which supports embedded provider blocks
Pin the module with `version = "~> 1.0"` so the provider block is ignored
quiz.explain: A module that contains its own provider blocks cannot use count, for_each or depends_on, so the configuration must come from the root. Choice C is wrong because for_each has the same limit, and choices B and D do not touch the cause.

days.recap: Extract modules for reuse and encoded decisions, never for pass-through wrappers; accept inputs rather than create what the caller owns and keep the tree flat. Use moved blocks for address changes, keep provider blocks in the root, and treat outputs and semantic versions as the contract.

days.title: Registry and terraform test: Version Selection, Publishing, Private Registry, Mocks and Run Blocks

concepts.heading: Module Sources and Version Selection
concepts.body: The `version` argument takes a constraint and works only for modules from a registry, the public Terraform Registry or an HCP Terraform private registry; local paths share the caller's repository and Git sources are not versioned this way. A call with `source = "git::https://git.example.com/net.git"` and `version = "1.2.0"` makes `terraform init` fail. For Git, select a revision with the `ref` query parameter (a tag, branch or commit SHA), as in `?ref=v1.2.0`; without `ref`, Terraform clones the default branch at HEAD, which changes over time. Module versions are not recorded in `.terraform.lock.hcl`, which covers provider selections and checksums only. Terraform uses the newest installed module version that meets the constraint; if an acceptable one is already installed, a plain `terraform init` keeps it, and with none installed (a fresh checkout or CI runner) it downloads the newest allowed. With `version = "~> 2.1"`, a laptop initialized when 2.4.0 was newest stays on 2.4.0 while CI selects 2.5.0 after it is published. `terraform init -upgrade` moves installed modules to the latest allowed version. Where reproducibility matters, pin an exact version.

concepts.heading: Publishing to the Public Registry
concepts.body: The public registry publishes modules directly from a public GitHub repository. Requirements: the repository is named `terraform-<PROVIDER>-<NAME>` (for example `terraform-aws-ec2-instance`, and NAME may contain hyphens), it has a short description, it follows the standard module structure with the root module's `.tf` files at the repository root, and it has release tags that are semantic versions, optionally prefixed with `v`. At least one such tag is needed to publish; tags that do not look like versions are ignored. A repository called `aws-vpc-module` with tags like `release-2024.03` therefore needs two changes: rename it to the required pattern and create semantic version tags such as `v1.0.0`. New versions appear when a correctly formed tag is pushed and the registry's webhook notifies it. The standard module structure is conventional: `main.tf`, `variables.tf` and `outputs.tf` plus `README.md` and `LICENSE` at the root; `modules/` holds nested modules, where one with a `README.md` is intended for external use and one without is internal; `examples/` holds example configurations. Calls to nested modules from the root should use relative paths such as `./modules/consul-cluster` so they stay part of the same package. This layout is advisory and Terraform does not enforce it.

concepts.heading: Private Registry Addressing and Monorepos
concepts.body: A registry source has the form `<NAMESPACE>/<NAME>/<PROVIDER>`, and without a hostname Terraform uses the public registry. A private registry adds the hostname in front. For HCP Terraform the hostname is `app.terraform.io` and the namespace is the organization name, so module `vpc` for provider `aws` in organization `acme` is `app.terraform.io/acme/vpc/aws`, selected within 1.x from 1.4 with `version = "~> 1.4"`. Callers need credentials for the registry, for example from `terraform login`, but not access to the module's source repository. When one repository holds `modules/app` and `modules/db` and is published by tag, every valid semantic-version tag creates a version of both modules, so releasing app also releases db. The fix is the Module Tag Prefix: with prefix `app-`, the tag `app-v1.0.0` publishes version `v1.0.0` of app only, and db ignores it. The Source Directory setting tells the registry where each module's files are but does not decide which tags apply. HCP Terraform can also run a module's tests automatically, but only for modules published with the branch-based workflow (a branch and a version, no tag required); it then runs on every commit to the branch and is unavailable while the organization publishes from a single repository. Engineers can run the stored tests with `terraform test -cloud-run=`.

concepts.heading: Mocks and Overrides in terraform test
concepts.body: A mocked provider (`mock_provider "aws" {}`) returns the real provider's schema and fills computed attributes with fake data, by type: numbers are 0, booleans false and strings random 8-character alphanumeric values. By default that data is generated during apply, so in a `command = plan` run computed attributes remain unknown (known after apply) and an assertion like `aws_s3_bucket.logs.arn != ""` cannot be evaluated. Setting `override_during = plan` on the mock makes Terraform generate data at plan time, and the attribute can also appear in `mock_resource`, `mock_data` and override blocks, which win over the provider-level setting. The mock does not know real formats. A module with a precondition on `startswith(aws_iam_role.r.arn, "arn:aws:iam::")` fails under the generic mock, so give the attribute a realistic value with `mock_resource "aws_iam_role" { defaults = { arn = "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/test" } }`. Defaults can also live in `.tfmock.hcl` files. For modules, `override_resource` and `override_data` replace the computed values of a specific instance, and `override_module` with `outputs` replaces a whole module's outputs while Terraform creates none of that module's resources. This is how root-level assertions run without cloud credentials or S3 calls. Overrides can sit at file level or in a run block, where run level wins.

concepts.heading: Run Blocks: Failure Tests, Parallelism, Variables and Cleanup
concepts.body: `expect_failures` lists checkable objects (resources, data sources, `check` blocks, input variables, outputs) whose custom conditions are expected to fail; the run passes if they fail. Only the author's `validation`, `precondition`, `postcondition` and `check` conditions count, so a type mismatch still fails the run. By default run blocks execute one after another. With `parallel = true` on the `test` block or a run block, two runs execute together only if neither references the other's outputs, they use different state files, and both allow parallelism. The state file is chosen by `state_key` or, if unset, by module source, so independent runs against the main configuration share one state and gain no speed until each has its own `state_key`. At the end of a file Terraform destroys everything it created in reverse run block order, using the last run block that referenced each state: with setup (bucket module), init (main) and read (loader module) in that order, it destroys read's state, then main, then setup's, so the bucket is not deleted while objects remain. For variables, usual precedence applies except that values defined in the test file, file-level or run-level, are highest and override `-var`, variable files and environment variables, so `terraform test -var region=eu-west-1` loses to `variables { region = "us-east-1" }` in the file unless the run block sets its own value.

examPoints: A question that combines a Git source with a version argument is testing that version works only for registry modules; Git revisions use ref.
A question about a mocked test that cannot evaluate a computed attribute is testing override_during = plan, and a question about format-sensitive conditions is testing mock_resource defaults.
A question about parallel run blocks that gain nothing is testing separate state_key values and absent output references; about test variables, values in the test file win.

quiz.q: A module call has `version = "~> 2.1"`. A laptop was initialized when 2.4.0 was the newest release. 2.5.0 is now published and a CI job starts from a fresh checkout. With no extra flags, what do `terraform init` on the laptop and in CI select?
choices: Both select 2.5.0 because `.terraform.lock.hcl` records the newest module version
Both keep 2.4.0 because the constraint pins the installed minor version
The laptop selects 2.1.0 and CI selects 2.5.0 because init always picks the oldest matching version when no flag is given
The laptop keeps 2.4.0 and CI downloads 2.5.0, since module versions are not locked and an installed acceptable version is kept
quiz.explain: The lock file covers providers only, and plain init keeps an acceptable installed module while a fresh runner downloads the newest allowed. Choices A and B assume a lock that does not exist, and C describes behaviour Terraform does not have.

quiz.q: A test file sets `test { parallel = true }` and has four independent run blocks against the same module directory, with no `state_key` and no `module` blocks. It takes the same time as before. What is the reason and the fix?
choices: Run blocks never run in parallel when `command = plan` is used; switch to apply
They share the main configuration's state, so give each run block its own `state_key`
Parallelism needs `-parallelism=4` on the CLI; the test block setting is advisory
Parallel runs need `override_during = plan` on the mock provider
quiz.explain: Runs that share a state file execute sequentially, and state_key separates them. Choice A is wrong because plan runs can be parallel, choice C confuses the apply flag with the test setting, and choice D concerns mock data timing.

days.recap: The version argument is for registries only; Git uses ref and module versions are not locked. Public publishing needs terraform-PROVIDER-NAME, semantic tags and the standard layout; monorepos need tag prefixes. In terraform test, plan-time mocks, realistic defaults, overrides, state_key and test-file variables decide results.

days.title: Operating HCP Terraform: Execution Modes, Agents, Run Tasks, Workflows and VCS Triggers

concepts.heading: Execution Modes and Changing Them
concepts.body: A workspace has an execution mode that decides where Terraform runs. Remote: HCP Terraform runs plan and apply on its own disposable workers, and variables, variable sets, policies, cost estimation, notifications and VCS integration all work. Agent: the same lifecycle, executed by a `tfc-agent` in your network. Local: Terraform runs on your machine and the workspace only stores state. Project Default: the workspace inherits the mode from its project. Local mode has a consequence that shows up as a puzzling error: when credentials live in a variable set but the workspace is Local, an engineer's `terraform plan` fails with a provider credential error (for AWS, `no valid credential sources`), because HCP Terraform has nothing to inject into a process on the workstation. A plan belongs to the platform that made it, so changing the mode after planning breaks it: a team that switches a busy workspace from Remote to Agent finds that two runs which had finished planning fail on confirmation. Runs still queued have not planned and are unaffected. The safe sequence is to disable auto-apply, finish or discard any run that is no longer pending, lock the workspace, change the mode and pool, then re-enable auto-apply and unlock.

concepts.heading: Agents and Agent Hooks
concepts.body: An HCP Terraform agent (`tfc-agent`) runs inside a private network, belongs to an agent pool, and polls HCP Terraform for work. A workspace in Agent mode sends its plan and apply jobs to an available agent in the chosen pool. This is the answer for provisioning vSphere resources in a data center that accepts no inbound connections: the agent needs only outbound TCP connections, to the HCP Terraform APIs, the module registry, `releases.hashicorp.com` for Terraform binaries and the providers' own APIs (here the local vCenter). No inbound firewall rule is needed and runs keep variables, policies and notifications. Agent hooks are executables the agent runs at fixed points: `pre-plan`, `post-plan`, `pre-apply` and `post-apply`. The file name must be `terraform-` plus one of those four (for example `terraform-pre-plan`), so an agent has at most one hook per type. Each hook must be executable and has a timeout (60 seconds by default, at most 10 minutes). The pre-plan and pre-apply hooks run before `terraform init` in their operation. A non-zero exit code or a timeout fails the run. Environment variables do not carry from one hook to the next; to pass a variable to the Terraform command of the same operation, write `KEY=value` lines to the file named by `$TFC_AGENT_ENV` rather than using a plain export.

concepts.heading: Run Tasks: Stages and Enforcement
concepts.body: Run tasks send a payload with a callback URL to an external service at pre-plan, post-plan, pre-apply or post-apply. The service must acknowledge with `200 OK` and then answer with `passed`, `running` or `failed`. The request errors if no progress update arrives within 10 minutes, and HCP Terraform treats a timeout or an unexpected remote error as failed. The enforcement level turns the result into an action: advisory shows a warning and the run continues, while mandatory stops the run with an error on failure, including timeout or remote error. A mandatory post-plan scanner whose service is down therefore blocks every run that reaches that stage. When a run has several tasks, the most restrictive result applies. The stage decides the data: pre-plan runs before any plan exists, so its payload carries only the configuration version, while post-plan payloads include the JSON of the plan, which is what a scanner that analyzes planned changes needs. Run tasks call an external service you or a vendor operate; rules written and evaluated inside HCP Terraform are policy as code, covered on day 19.

concepts.heading: Three Workflows
concepts.body: A workspace is driven in one of three ways. VCS-driven: the workspace links to a branch of a repository, webhooks queue a run on each merge and pull requests get speculative plans, which cannot be applied; the code always comes from version control. CLI-driven: engineers run `terraform plan` or `apply` with a `cloud` block and the run executes in the workspace, so remote applies and saved plans work without a linked repository. API-driven: no repository is linked; your tooling decides when a run happens, packages the configuration as a `.tar.gz` with the configuration directory at the archive root, creates a configuration version through the API, uploads the archive and then creates the run. A pipeline that generates Terraform configuration from an internal service catalog and keeps no Git repository fits the API-driven workflow. With the CLI-driven workflow the Terraform version that executes a remote run is the workspace's version setting, not the engineer's local binary; the local binary is only the client.

concepts.heading: VCS Triggers: Paths, Tags and the First Run
concepts.body: When a VCS-backed workspace has a working directory, HCP Terraform uses it as the default filter and assumes only changes inside matter. In a monorepo with workspace working directory `envs/prod`, a change to a shared module under `modules/` starts no run. The Automatic Run Triggering options are: always trigger runs for any change (simple, but queues unneeded runs); trigger only when files in specified paths change, using patterns (globs, recommended) or prefixes (directories, including the working directory), and the same filter applies to speculative plans on pull requests; or trigger on git tags. The fix for the monorepo is to add a pattern or prefix covering `modules/`. Tag triggering needs the tag in one of these formats: semantic version (the whole tag, such as `0.4.2`), version with a prefix (`release-1.4.0`), with a suffix (`0.4.2-alpha`), or a custom regular expression. A production workspace that runs only when a release such as `release-1.4.0` is cut therefore uses the prefix format. One more rule: a new workspace with no runs does not accept runs from a VCS webhook, so several merged commits with an empty run list and no error under VCS events usually mean no one has started the initial run manually. A workspace also ignores a webhook for a commit SHA that it already created a run for.

examPoints: A question about runs failing with no credential sources on a laptop is testing Local execution mode, where workspace variables and variable sets are not injected.
A question about a closed data center is testing agents: outbound-only connections from the agent pool, and no inbound rule; mandatory run tasks fail the run on timeout.
A question about no run starting after a shared module change is testing working directory filtering, and an empty run list on a new workspace points to the manual initial run.
